„Manche reiben sich eh schon seit jeher an Kimmich“. Joshua Kimmich ist vor dem Spiel in der UEFA Nations League in Griechenland wieder Thema auf der Pressekonferenz mit Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp gewesen. Der DFB-Kapitän wird wie auch gegen Serbien nicht dabei sein, weil er nicht zum „Kader 2“ gehört. „Für mich ist es ein Weltklasse-Spieler, ein ganz ganz zentraler Spieler und für Jürgen Klopp auch“, sagt unser Reporter Julien Wolff.

Sollten Kinder schon die Abnehmspritze bekommen?. Immer mehr Erwachsene setzen auf Abnehmspritzen. Inzwischen sind zwei Medikamente auch für Kinder und Jugendliche zugelassen. Doch was auf den ersten Blick nach einer einfachen Lösung klingt, wirft Fragen auf.

Die feinen Unterschiede der grünen Empörungskultur. In der Berliner Linkspartei wird dem Antisemitismus gefrönt, die grünen Sittenwächter fallen jedoch mit lautem Schweigen auf. Aber die nächste Menschenkette gegen rechts kommt bestimmt.

„Hatte das Gefühl, Teil meines Lebenszwecks und meiner Identität verloren zu haben“. Prinz Harry versucht sich nach seiner Rückkehr nach Großbritannien an einem Comeback – vor allem durch sein Engagement für Veteranen. Nun erzählt er, wie es ihm selbst erging, als er das Militär verlassen musste.

Auch Vorzeigekonzern BMW bleibt nicht verschont. BMW reagiert auf sinkende Gewinne und startet einen Konzernumbau. 8000 Stellen in Verwaltung und Entwicklung fallen weg, unrentable Modelle werden gestrichen und die Produktion stärker lokalisiert.

Wenn die Eltern ins Heim kommen – und die heikle Frage, wer zukünftig zahlt. Die Pflegekosten laufen aus dem Ruder. Die Regierung überlegt, erwachsene Kinder stärker als zuletzt zur Kasse zu bitten. Das schafft Verunsicherung bis tief in die Mittelschicht.

Touristen im Taxi von Sturzflut mitgerissen – Evakuierungen nach schweren Unwettern auf Kreta. Zerstörte Straßen, überschwemmte Häuser und Strände voller Trümmer. Die Urlaubsinsel Kreta wurde von einem schweren Unwetter getroffen. In einem beliebten Ausflugsziel stecken noch immer sechs Mitarbeiter fest.

„Klopp nimmt die Leute mit, Nagelsmann brachte sie gegen sich auf“. Rekordnationalspieler Lothar Matthäus bescheinigt Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp mehr Nähe zu Spielern und Fans als Julian Nagelsmann. Klopp liefere, sagt der RTL-Experte, klare Erklärungen und zeige Respekt.

Nächster Dämpfer für Alba – Niederlage im Klassiker gegen Bamberg. Meister Alba Berlin kassiert den nächsten Dämpfer in der Basketball-Bundesliga. Nach der Klatsche beim FC Bayern verliert der Meister auch den Klassiker gegen die Bamberg Baskets. Es ist das 138. Duell zwischen Berlin und Bamberg in der BBL und damit die am häufigsten gespielte Partie. Die Highlights im Video.

„Absolute Schande“ – Argentiniens Gegner verweigern Reise zum Spiel. Die Nationalmannschaft von Burkina Faso strandet auf dem Weg nach Argentinien in Marokko. Fast alle Spieler entscheiden sich gegen eine Weiterreise. Der Verband reagiert umgehend.

Iran knüpft Öffnung von Hormus an sieben Bedingungen. Die Führung in Teheran koppelt die Öffnung einer der wichtigsten Handelsrouten der Welt an maximale Zugeständnisse aus Washington. Ein Durchbruch gilt derzeit als unwahrscheinlich.

Erlösung für Verstappen – Russell-Drama hinter dem Safety-Car. Max Verstappen feiert in einem von chaotischen Verhältnissen geprägten Rennen in Malaysia seinen ersten Saisonsieg. Im Kampf um die WM erlebt Mercedes-Mann George Russell einen bitteren Moment.

„Die Illusion, dass bei BMW alles so viel besser läuft, bricht jetzt zusammen“. BMW streicht Stellen, senkt seine Gewinnprognose und setzt auf einen harten Sparkurs. Für WELT-Wirtschaftsjournalist Christoph Kapalschinski markiert der Kurswechsel das Ende einer jahrelang gepflegten Erfolgserzählung.

„Wir werden alle gemeinsam sterben“ – Dann wurde sie vollkommen ruhig. Als der Flydubai-Flug FZ1073 in den Sturzflug ging, bereiteten sich alle an Bord auf ihren Tod vor. Die Israelin Galit Gindi erzählt WELT, warum sie trotzdem ganz ruhig blieb. Und was sie nach der Notlandung in Saudi-Arabien überraschte.

„Herr Putin, hören Sie diesen sinnlosen Krieg auf“. Bei einem Besuch in Kiew sichert Kanzler Friedrich Merz Präsident Selenskyj weitere deutsche Unterstützung zu. Währenddessen steht die ukrainische Hauptstadt weiter unter Beschuss. Mit einer direkten Botschaft an Putin fordert Merz: „Die Waffen müssen schweigen.“

Der bizarre Fetisch linker Frauen, die Verehrung wollen. Dieses Weib hat für immer ausgelockt: Freundinnen der Rotfront können sich gern in Problemvierteln nach Partnern umsehen. Im bürgerlichen Kontext sind sie, pardon, unvermittelbar.

„Bis zu 40 Prozent der Arbeitszeit eingespart“ – OpenAIs Botschaft an den Mittelstand. Die rasante Entwicklung der KI verändert nicht nur die Möglichkeiten, sondern auch die Gefahren der Technologie. OpenAIs Europachef erklärt, wie seiner Meinung nach Menschen die Kontrolle behalten können – und wie ChatGPT aktuell in Deutschland genutzt wird.

Ich testete die 480-Euro-Zahnbürste mit eingebauter Kamera – so gut ist sie wirklich. Mit einer integrierten Mini-Kamera und KI will Dyson die Alltags-Zahnpflege revolutionieren. Im Test zeigt sich, was an dem Luxus-Gerät fasziniert – und an welche Grenzen die Technik stößt.

41 Prozent der Berliner sprechen sich für Koalition unter Elif Eralp aus. Trotz Antisemitismusvorwürfen und Kontakten ins Clan-Milieu wünscht sich eine relative Mehrheit der Berliner eine neue Landesregierung unter Führung der Linken. Vor allem Bundeskanzler Merz spielt dabei eine Rolle.

Waldbrand breitet sich bei Santa Clarita rasant aus. In der Nähe von Los Angeles brennt ein Waldgebiet bei Santa Clarita. Das Feuer hat bereits 400 Hektar erfasst. Behörden rufen Anwohner auf, sich in Sicherheit zu bringen.

„Das medial überragende Thema ist Korruption“. Brasilien geht tief gespalten in die Präsidentschaftswahl. Für WELT-Korrespondent Tobias Käufer wird der Wahlkampf vor allem von Korruptionsvorwürfen gegen das oberste Gericht überschattet.

Transportkosten von 1,35 Millionen Euro nicht bezahlt – Geldgeberin wegen offener Rechnung verklagt. Die Walrettung in der Ostsee landet nun auch vor Gericht: Ein Unternehmer verklagt die Geldgeberin auf mehr als eine Million Euro. Er ist nicht der Einzige, der noch auf Geld wartet. Karin Walter-Mommert verweist auf Mängel bei der Leistung des Unternehmens.

Zwischen Romanautor und Leser besteht eine persönliche Beziehung, ein „autografischer Pakt“. Wird ein Roman als KI-Produkt enttarnt, ist die Empörung riesig. Aber warum eigentlich? Um zu verstehen, warum sich Leser getäuscht, sogar verraten fühlen, hilft das alte Konzept eines französischen Literaturwissenschaftlers.

‘What Is Happening Today Is Development in Reverse’. A conversation with UNDP chief Alexander De Croo about building infrastructure in active conflict zones.
What’s at Stake in Brazil’s Election. Results would have broad implications on foreign policy.
The Trauma Plot to Destroy America. A new book examines how narratives about psychological harm have come to dominate public life.
What in the World?. Test yourself on the week of Sept. 26: Trump pressures Zelensky, Venezuelans protest, and Morocco picks a new prime minister.
The Illicit World of Sea Cucumbers. How a rare delicacy in Asia drives crime oceans away.
Where Does Russia’s Violent Imperialism Come From?. A new book provides some helpful—if not always spot-on—answers.
G-7 Agrees to Release 100 Million Barrels of Reserve Diesel. The White House had threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports if Europe did not step up.
The Year Hollywood Changed the National Security Debate. In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of new technologies.

The body as a battleground: Iran's resistance etched in ink and blood. After the Islamic Republic turned its guns on protesters during Iran’s nationwide January uprising, filling streets, hospitals and morgues with the wounded and the dead, it may have silenced the streets, but protest and dissent have found a new battleground: the body.

US blockade divides Iranians online over pressure on rulers, cost to public. Iran’s deepening isolation is drawing divided reactions from Persian-language social media users, with some welcoming US pressure to weaken the country’s rulers and others warning that ordinary people will bear the cost without producing political change.

German-based aid worker gets 10-year prison sentence in Iran. A German-based humanitarian worker has been sentenced to 10 years in prison in Iran after entering the country to help vulnerable Iranians, Stuttgart-based aid organization STELP said.

Iranian hardliners turn on Ghalibaf and judiciary after lawmaker’s sentencing. Attacks by hardliners on Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf and Chief Justice Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei following hardline lawmaker Hamid Rasaei’s imprisonment have intensified the rift among Iran’s conservatives.

Iran debtors face prison, hiding and suicide attempts. Years in prison or hiding, suicide attempts and severe financial hardship are among the consequences of Iran’s imprisonment of people over unpaid financial obligations, according to an IHRDC report published Tuesday.

Flydubai flight diverts to Saudi Arabia after suspected cockpit stabbing. Both pilots of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv were injured after what Israeli officials said may have been an attempted terror attack in the cockpit, forcing the aircraft to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday.

Iran death-row protester shot, tortured in custody. Iranian security forces shot death-row protester Alireza Sepahi four times during his arrest at home before subjecting him to weeks of torture in custody, according to a former cellmate who described his treatment.

Iran takes US response to cabinet, Hormuz clashes continue. Iran took a US response to its latest diplomatic proposal to cabinet, a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and two January protesters were executed among the key developments on Wednesday.

‘I never asked about regime change’: Student speaks out after El-Sayed exchange. An Iranian-American student who pressed Michigan Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to state his position on Iran’s Revolutionary Guards says he and his family have faced threats and harassment after a video of the exchange went viral.

US ‘feedback’ leaves Iran debating the price of diplomacy. Iran’s receipt of Washington’s response to its seven-point proposal for ending the Strait of Hormuz crisis has sharpened divisions in Tehran over whether to pursue further compromise or intensify pressure on the United States.

Prisoners beaten, kept in windowless cells at Isfahan prison. Prisoners in a security ward at Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan are beaten with cables and metal rods and held in overcrowded, windowless cells with poor ventilation, according to accounts provided to Iran International.

UK points to Iran role in suspected plot near RAF Fairford. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there are “strong indications” Iran played a role in a suspected plot near RAF Fairford airbase used by US forces to carry out strikes on the Islamic Republic.

Tehran weighs what comes next if US diplomacy fails. Continued contacts between Tehran and Washington, mediated by Qatar and Pakistan, have intensified debate inside Iran over whether diplomacy can still produce a deal despite President Donald Trump’s rejection of Tehran’s latest proposal and what should happen if it fails.

Iran official warns Starlink could end state control of internet. The spread of Starlink could deliver the “final nail in the coffin” of Iran’s ability to control cyberspace, Deputy Communications Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami said Wednesday, even as authorities seek to suppress the technology through arrests, seizures and criminal penalties.

Iran turns to younger children in postwar ideological push. The Basij has long maintained a presence in Iran's high schools and universities. Its growing visibility among much younger children is drawing attention to a new front in the Islamic Republic's effort to shape a generation that has repeatedly challenged its authority.

IRGC says six gunmen killed in clash in Iran's restive southeast. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said six gunmen were killed on Thursday in an hours-long clash with security forces in southeastern Iran, the latest in a series of armed confrontations in the restive Sistan-Baluchestan province.

Iranian weapons, Chinese supplies fuel Houthi advance in Yemen - WSJ. Iranian weapons and growing supplies of Chinese dual-use components have helped Yemen's Houthis expand their territory and strengthen their ability to threaten shipping through the Red Sea, the Wall Street Journal reported.

670 bridges, 380 tunnels: The network that moves Iran's army and its missiles. Four small bridges, struck in one night in April, cut Tehran off from Iran's entire railway. All were fixed within days. The bridges that would take years to rebuild are still standing, on lines that carry Iran's missiles, its troops and its trade.

Trump says renewed bombing of Iran after midterms 'possible'. US President Donald Trump said renewed large-scale bombing of Iran after the November midterm elections was "possible," while rejecting Tehran's latest ceasefire proposal as insufficient, according to an interview with TIME published on Thursday.

Iran sentences 20-year-old blogger to more than 13 years in prison. Iranian authorities have sentenced 20-year-old blogger Iman Sadeghi, who was arrested in Kashan during the nationwide protests earlier this year, to more than 13 years in prison, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Iran oil exports vanish as regional flows surpass prewar levels. New tanker-tracking data shows that Iran’s new oil exports have effectively ground to a halt, while crude exports from Arab countries in the region surpassed pre-war levels in the final week of September.

Four January protest detainees sentenced to death by Tehran courts. Four men detained during Iran’s nationwide January protests have been sentenced to death by Tehran Revolutionary Courts, HRANA reported Thursday, as rights groups warn of mounting use of capital punishment against protest detainees.

US targets Iran auto, rail and metals sectors in new sanctions blitz. The US Treasury sanctioned Iran’s automotive and rail sectors Thursday, expanding its campaign to some of the country’s largest industrial companies as Washington seeks to choke off Tehran’s sources of revenue with Operation Economic Outcast.

Iran links under scrutiny in separate Flydubai, UK airbase investigations. Iran on Thursday was linked by US and Israeli officials to the Flydubai incident, the second such case after British police opened a probe into possible Tehran involvement in a suspected RAF Fairford plot and arrested a dual UK-Iranian national.

Leaked Kremlin plan undercuts Moscow's claims on ruble-rial trade with Iran. A leaked Russian government roadmap obtained by Fox News put the share of Russia-Iran trade settled in national currencies at 68%, far below Moscow’s public claims that nearly all bilateral trade had shifted to rubles and rials.

Iranian press sees diplomacy alive but narrowing after US response. Tehran media see diplomacy with Washington as increasingly precarious but not yet dead, with the two sides far apart over the sequencing of any deal and the window for compromise appearing to narrow.

Iran's rhetoric against UAE hardens after Netanyahu visit. Iranian officials and media have sharply condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the UAE, warning Abu Dhabi over its deepening ties with Israel amid renewed tensions over three disputed Persian Gulf islands.

A Mossad spy in Iran: From banking infiltration to nuclear and missile sabotage. A former Mossad agent says he spent years inside one of Iran's best-known telecom businesses, using its banking tricks to fund Israeli operations and deleting a file from a switch near Malard minutes before the 2011 blast that killed the father of Iran's missile program.

Can the Caspian give Iran a way around Hormuz?. With war disrupting Iran’s southern trade routes, Tehran is looking north to the Caspian for alternatives. But the available evidence suggests they cannot replace its crucial oil exports.

Al-Qaeda is Iran's quiet backup if the war turns, expert says. Iran has spent two decades keeping al-Qaeda close as a partner it can deny, and could turn to it if the war with the United States escalates, a counterterrorism expert told Iran International. With Hezbollah and Hamas weakened, she said, it is the card Tehran has left.

Iran’s truck repair hub feels the squeeze as work dries up. Business at one of central Iran’s main heavy-vehicle service hubs has fallen by about 30% from a year earlier, offering a ground-level view of an economy where soaring food prices, a battered currency and weaker freight activity are squeezing workers and small businesses.

Shot in leg, forced into hiding: Iran protester recounts January crackdown. Hamid Kouhsari was carrying a wounded woman on his back through the streets of Gorgan on January 8 when security forces shot him from behind. He spent the next eight months in hiding with his leg untreated, before leaving Iran.

Five killed in roadside attack as violence spreads in southeast Iran. At least five people were reported killed on Friday in an attack near Zahedan in southeastern Iran, as the Revolutionary Guards confirmed a roadside bombing in the area that killed one of its fighters.

Iran court upholds film star’s jail term over post mourning protest victims. An appeals court in Tehran has upheld a one-year prison sentence for renowned actress Elnaz Shakerdoost over an Instagram story mourning people killed during January’s protests, her lawyer said Friday.

As the rial sinks, Iranians seek shelter in almost anything else. Iran’s stock market is breaking records even as the dollar and gold hit new highs, an apparent contradiction that may point to the same dynamic: households and investors scrambling to protect their wealth as the rial weakens and the economic toll of the Iran-US war grows.

Iran denies teachers are quitting despite viral resignation videos. Iran’s Education Ministry dismissed reports of teacher resignations over working conditions and security pressure as a “rumor,” despite numerous videos of teachers announcing departures and a teachers’ council warning of a growing exodus.

Two Iranians charged over foiled plot targeting Manchester Jews. Two Iranian men have been charged over a terrorist plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community that was disrupted before it could be carried out, British police said Friday.

'They shot on sight': Amnesty details 2022 protest killings in Kurdish areas. Iranian security forces shot civilians at close range, pursued fleeing protesters and prevented wounded people from receiving help during the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising in Kurdish cities, according to Amnesty International’s investigation into the crackdown.

Officials trade blame as Iran’s economy sinks deeper. Iran’s worsening economic crisis has opened an increasingly bitter argument over who is responsible, as the government points to outside pressure and market psychology while hardliners accuse Tehran’s own economic officials of making the situation worse.

Iran executes man arrested during January protests. Iran has executed Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, who was arrested during January’s protests in Shahrekord, the judiciary’s Mizan news agency announced Saturday.

Islamic Republic's 'slow meltdown' leaves it fewer ways out, analysts say. The Islamic Republic is in a "slow meltdown" that may not bring it down soon but is narrowing its options as the economy sinks, repression deepens and divisions open up among its own hardliners, analysts told Iran International's Eye for Iran podcast.

Smartwatches on Iran's security chiefs spark row within the inner circle. Senior Iranian military and security officials have been photographed wearing smartwatches, drawing fresh criticism of their basic security discipline after years of reports that Israel has used electronic devices around Iranian commanders to track and kill them.

Euro tops 3 million rials as Iran's currency hits fresh record lows. Iran's rial fell to new record lows on Saturday, with the euro crossing 3 million rials for the first time and the US dollar hovering around 2.7 million rials on the open market.

'The end of illness is not treatment. It is death': Iranian MP on the cost of care. Iranians are selling livestock, cars and furniture to pay for treatment their insurance no longer covers, and a member of parliament's health committee says the system has reached the point where falling ill can end in death rather than care.

Khamenei adviser warns UAE as tensions with Tehran escalate. A senior adviser to Iran’s supreme leader issued a pointed warning to the United Arab Emirates on Saturday, saying “imported security has an expiration date” as tensions between Tehran and Abu Dhabi continue to rise.

Iranian women break records and barriers at Asian Games. Iranian women have delivered a record-breaking performance at the 2026 Asian Games, winning medals across an unusually broad range of sports and achieving a series of firsts for the country.

Security meeting, military buildup: US weighs next move on Iran?. An unannounced meeting of President Donald Trump’s senior national security team at Camp David, as another aircraft carrier and thousands more US troops move toward the Middle East, has raised the prospect of another major operation against Iran.

Iran demolishes prison despite warnings of erasing evidence of mass killings. One of the last watchtowers at Iran’s Rajaei Shahr (Gohardasht) prison was demolished Saturday, as authorities dismantle a site of mass political executions despite longstanding warnings that its destruction could erase evidence of crimes against humanity.

Trump weighs Iran decision with ‘all options’ on the table. US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was approaching a decision on Iran, warning Tehran faced the “easy way or the hard way” as the Pentagon kept military options open amid continued attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian currency hits another record low under US economic pressure. Iran’s currency fell to another record low against the dollar on Sunday, extending its decline during a US campaign aimed at restricting the Islamic Republic’s oil exports and financial flows.

Maroc : le PAM saura-t-il relever le défi du pouvoir ?. Convaincre les abstentionnistes, bâtir une coalition qui ne soit pas une simple distribution de postes, donner un sens à la victoire électorale du 23 septembre : pour la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement, Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, le plus difficile commence.

L’or et le lithium du Mali dans le viseur de l’administration Trump. Une vingtaine d’invités, des experts du secteur minier et de la sécurité, et, surtout, la plus grande discrétion. Le 24 septembre, à Bamako, un panel organisé par l’ambassade des États-Unis a posé les premiers jalons d’une offensive de Washington sur les ressources minières maliennes.

Hausse du SMIG, baisse des impôts… Au Maroc, la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement a-t-elle les moyens de ses ambitions sociales ?. Le gouvernement Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri porte un agenda social inédit, promettant un million d’emplois et des retraites minimales à 3 000 dirhams. Reste à financer un programme aussi ambitieux.

Au Ghana, le retour au calme à Bawku signe-t-il vraiment le recul de la violence jihadiste venue du Burkina Faso ?. Bawku connaît un calme inédit : plus de 130 jours sans violence, dans une ville meurtrie par des décennies de conflits ethniques. Médiation, pression sécuritaire et lassitude des communautés expliquent ce fragile répit. Analyse.

Interdiction des importations françaises: un pas de plus dans la crise franco-algérienne. Applicable depuis juillet 2026 mais sans avoir fait l’objet d’une communication officielle auprès des entreprises concernées, l’interdiction d’importer des marchandises françaises met de nombreux partenaires algériens en difficulté. Et vient encore dégrader une relation déjà glaciale.

Pétrole : pourquoi Abidjan invite Murphy Oil à intensifier ses forages. Après avoir fait de l’offshore ivoirien sa porte d’entrée sur le continent en attendant d’étendre ses opérations au Maroc et au Cameroun via de nouveaux permis, Murphy Oil fait déjà face à un premier test décisif proposé par Abidjan.

RDC : Walter Mbonyimwami fait le pari de l’IA pour explorer les mines du continent. Alors que la RDC abrite 70 % des réserves mondiales de cobalt et est le premier producteur de cuivre en Afrique, la start-up Synchros s’est fixé pour objectif de rationaliser l’exploitation minière grâce à la technologie numérique.

10 choses à savoir sur Justin Koné Katinan, bras droit de Laurent Gbagbo derrière les barreaux. Quatrième vice-président du PPA-CI, l’ancien ministre a été placé sous mandat de dépôt pour « actes de terrorisme ». Portrait d’un fidèle de longue date de Gbagbo, contraint à l’exil pendant plus d’une décennie, qui n’en est pas à sa première interpellation.

RDC : Denise Dusauchoy, itinéraire d’une influenceuse sous influence. Arrêtée en Tanzanie le 30 août, l’influenceuse est détenue depuis un mois par les services de renseignements congolais. Celle qui fut une sympathisante du président Félix Tshisekedi a fini par se mettre le pouvoir à dos.

Cameroun : pourquoi Vision 4, la chaîne de télévision d’Amougou Belinga, a été suspendue. Incarcéré depuis deux ans dans le cadre de l’affaire Martinez Zogo, du nom du journaliste tué à Yaoundé en 2023, Jean-Pierre Amougou Belinga voit sa chaîne de télévision privée d’antenne pour un mois par le Conseil national de la communication. Un nouveau bras de fer s’engage donc avec le régulateur.

RDC-France : de Kinshasa à Bunia, les enjeux de la visite de Jean-Noël Barrot. Le ministre français des Affaires étrangères se rend les 2 et 3 octobre en RDC, avant une conférence humanitaire à Paris. Il fera une étape, inédite pour le chef de la diplomatie française, dans l’est du pays.

Paiement instantané : Wave rallie la plateforme de la BCEAO et acte une nouvelle ère pour l’union monétaire. Avec sa plateforme de paiement instantanée, l’UEMOA entre dans l’ère du paiement interopérable entre banques et portefeuilles mobiles. Un bouleversement qui menace les revenus des opérateurs et redistribue les cartes.

États-Unis – Cameroun : Trump choisit l’artisan de ses accords d’expulsion comme ambassadeur à Yaoundé. Christian Jové Ehrhardt, responsable des très controversées expulsions de migrants vers des pays tiers, représente désormais Washington à Yaoundé. Une nomination qui éclaire les dessous de l’accord secret signé en décembre 2025 entre les États-Unis et le Cameroun.

Afrique du Sud, Algérie, Côte d’Ivoire, Égypte, Maroc : qui est prêt à jouer les plans B pour la CAN 2027 ?. Théoriquement, la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2027 doit se tenir en Ouganda, en Tanzanie et au Kenya. Mais face aux retards qui s’accumulent, la CAF a commencé à sonder certains pays. En tête de liste : le Maroc, l’Algérie et l’Afrique du Sud.

Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina, Mali… Le boom des raffineries d’or face au scepticisme des géants miniers. L’Afrique de l’ouest multiplie les raffineries d’or pour transformer sa matière première sur place. Si obliger les artisans miniers à y envoyer leur or est une gageure, encourager les industriels à le faire est encore plus difficile. Analyse.

Au Sénégal, Petrosen espère lancer Sangomar 2 à l’horizon 2028. Ce 1er octobre, le directeur général de Petrosen, Thierno Seydou Ly, a annoncé vouloir entrer dans le deuxième phase de Sangomar d’ici à 2028. L’objectif serait d’ajouter 8 puits supplémentaires.

Les six jours les plus longs : comment s’est décidée la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri à la primature marocaine. Le 23 septembre, le PAM arrive en tête des législatives. Mais passé les célébrations vient l’attente. Réserves religieuses, procès de personnalité, hypothèse Lekjaâ : récit des six jours durant lesquels une nomination qui semblait acquise a soudain cessé de l’être.

Aroni Chaudhuri (Coface) : « Le principal risque pour l’économie marocaine, c’est un risque social ». Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri prend les rênes d’un pays à l’économie solide mais qui éprouve des difficultés à réduire les inégalités. Aroni Chaudhuri, économiste chez Coface, passe en revue les défis qui attendent la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement.

Bénin : Romuald Wadagni attendu à Paris pour sa première visite officielle en France. Le président béninois sera à Paris les 4 et 5 octobre pour sa première « visite de travail » depuis son investiture à la tête du pays. Il doit notamment rencontrer son homologue, Emmanuel Macron.

Nucleon Security, la pépite qui défie les géants mondiaux de la cybersécurité. L’éditeur de solutions de cybersécurité veut intensifier son développement sur les marchés d’Afrique subsaharienne, certain de pouvoir se différencier des géants du secteur grâce à sa technologie et son adaptation au terrain.

Avec l’acquisition de Société générale Ghana, Attijariwafa Bank relance son expansion internationale, à pas comptés. Le rachat de Société générale Ghana marque une première incursion stratégique pour le groupe marocain en zone anglophone. Mais l’opération reste modeste et pourrait être confrontée aux aléas monétaires.

En Guinée équatoriale, une nouvelle vague d’expulsions relance le débat sur la libre circulation au sein de la Cemac. Les autorités équato-guinéennes multiplient les arrestations et expulsions d’étrangers originaires d’Afrique centrale. Au cœur des procédures : un différend sur l’application d’un accord signé dans le cadre de la Cemac.

Bras de fer chez Castel : la justice de Singapour relance la lutte pour le contrôle du géant de la bière. Alors que le groupe Castel est l’objet d’un conflit entre la fille du fondateur, Romy Castel, et l’actuel directeur général, Gregory Clerc, une décision de justice à Singapour relance les hostilités. Et pose autant de questions qu’elle donne de réponse.

« Tous les militaires avaient déjà pris le large » : en RDC, la justice militaire se penche sur la chute de Bukavu. Deux généraux, jugés depuis le 25 septembre dernier, sont accusés d’avoir abandonné la capitale du Sud-Kivu en février 2025, pendant l’offensive des rebelles de l’AFC/M23. Des pièces du dossier, obtenues par Jeune Afrique, lèvent le voile sur les dysfonctionnements de l’armée congolaise.

États-Unis – Afrique : comment Donald Trump tente de combler le vide dans les ambassades américaines. Le Congrès américain a validé la nomination de sept nouveaux ambassadeurs en Afrique. Une goutte d’eau, alors que plus de la moitié des postes diplomatiques restent vacants sur le continent après la purge opérée par Trump au début de son mandat. Cartographie.

La première femme nommée à la tête du gouvernement au Maroc, les juntes sahéliennes à l’ONU, l’après-Orano au Niger… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, première femme à la tête du gouvernement marocain, décrypte l’entourage de Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, analyse la stratégie diplomatique commune des juntes sahéliennes, examine la relance de l’uranium au Niger et s’intéresse au pari des solutions solaires pour électrifier l’Afrique rurale.

Avant Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, une longue lignée de militantes marocaines. S’il répond à une logique institutionnelle, le choix d’une femme, Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri, pour diriger le gouvernement issu des élections du 23 septembre reste un événement. Pourtant, d’autres avant elle ont déjà joué un rôle de premier plan dans l’histoire du royaume.

Afrique de l’Ouest : les véritables ressorts d’une inflation alimentaire tenace. Carburants, engrais, change et météo : les coûts de la chaîne alimentaire s’envolent à nouveau en Afrique de l’Ouest. Une crise structurelle, qui met en lumière les fragilités d’économies encore trop dépendantes des marchés mondiaux. Décryptage en infographies.

Gabon : ces femmes qui font l’économie. Secteur pétrolier, distribution, conseil… Au Gabon, de plus en plus de femmes sont aux commandes dans des secteurs économiques cruciaux. Jeune Afrique a choisi cinq trajectoires qui illustrent cette transformation en cours.

Maroc : ceux (et celles) qui murmurent à l’oreille de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri. Pour comprendre l’ascension de la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement, il faut regarder ceux qui l’entourent. Intimes, stratèges, équilibristes ou protégés, ils racontent aussi la trajectoire singulière du Parti Authenticité et Modernité (PAM) et les réseaux sur lesquels la femme politique pourra s’appuyer.

Dans le nord du Nigeria, le nombre d’enlèvements augmente sous la pression de gangs criminels locaux et des djihadistes. Au moins 87 personnes ont été kidnappées samedi et dimanche dans les Etats de Zamfara et du Niger. Entre juillet 2025 et juin 2026, on dénombrait 7 825 victimes de prises d’otage, un chiffre en hausse qui fragilise le pouvoir, avant l’élection présidentielle de janvier 2027.

Au Maroc, malgré la nomination d’une première ministre, le plafond de verre demeure pour les femmes. Sur 395 députés élus au Parlement après le scrutin du 23 septembre, la représentation des femmes reste minoritaire (107) et cantonnée aux quotas. Toutefois, la nomination de Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri par le roi suscite l’espoir des associations féministes.

En Algérie, les députés étendent la peine de mort aux auteurs de feux de forêt. Le texte élargit également la peine capitale à de nouveaux cas d’enlèvements d’enfants accompagnés de violences graves, les autorités évoquant une recrudescence de ces actes ces dernières années.

Pourquoi l’Ethiopie replonge-t-elle dans la guerre ? Comprendre en trois minutes. Après plusieurs mois de tensions, les combats ont repris à la fin de septembre en Ethiopie entre l’armée fédérale éthiopienne et différents groupes rebelles, laissant planer la menace d’un nouveau conflit de grande ampleur. Une guerre civile avait déjà éclaté dans le pays entre 2020 et 2022.

En Egypte, l’arrestation de six journalistes d’un média d’investigation, signe de la nervosité du régime du président Al-Sissi. Ce coup de force sans précédent arrive au moment où les autorités doivent faire face à un contexte économique tendu et à des rivalités politiques qui s’aiguisent pour succéder au président Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi, au pouvoir depuis 2013.

Au Kenya, le lancement en un temps record du chantier de la raffinerie Dangote. Le magnat nigérian Aliko Dangote ambitionne de répliquer sa raffinerie de Lagos à Lamu, une région isolée face à l’océan Indien. Mercredi 30 septembre, en présence de chefs d’Etat africains, s’est tenue une cérémonie hautement politique et symbolique.

Pourquoi l’Algérie a élargi la peine de mort aux incendiaires et aux kidnappeurs d’enfants. Après les feux de forêts intenses et meurtriers de l’été, le chef de l’Etat, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a souhaité élargir le nombre de « crimes capitaux », passibles de la peine de mort. Le pays respectait pourtant un moratoire sur cette question depuis 1993.

A Johannesburg, la découverte de onze corps révèle l’ampleur des violences à l’égard des femmes. Depuis juillet, des corps de femmes nues ou à moitié nues, violemment battues, ont été retrouvés en banlieue de Johannesburg. Si la thèse du prédateur en série s’amenuise, la réalité d’une extrême violence infligée aux Sud-Africaines au quotidien s’impose.

Guerre en Ethiopie : des attaques de drones ciblent la capitale, les forces gouvernementales gagnent du terrain dans le nord du pays. Après les frappes sur Addis-Abeba mercredi soir, le gouvernement éthiopien a décidé la fermeture de son ambassade à Asmara. En réponse, l’Erythrée a rompu tous ses liens diplomatiques avec l’Ethiopie.

Sur l’île idyllique de Lamu, au Kenya, l’arrivée d’une mégaraffinerie de pétrole est vue comme une opportunité économique autant qu’un péril écologique. Le lancement en grande pompe de ce colossal chantier du groupe nigérian Dangote a eu lieu mercredi 30 septembre sur le port isolé de Lamu, face à l’océan Indien. L’île du même nom, écrin touristique et berceau de la culture swahilie, retient son souffle.

Au Burkina Faso et au Mali, les juntes veulent tirer profit de la manne aurifère. La maîtrise de la chaîne de production de l’or permet aux régimes militaires de réaffirmer leur souveraineté nationale sur les ressources naturelles.

Ebola en RDC : le bilan de la pire épidémie de l’histoire du pays franchit 4 000 morts. Gaza Friendly: the French label turning consumer choices into Palestine solidarity Submitted by Tassa Adidi on Mon, 09/28/2026 - 15:10 In France, a unique app certifies shopkeepers boycotting products linked to Israeli settlements while promoting alternative brands Gaza Friendly, launched in 2025, is inspired by the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement (provided) Off Among the many apps available on the Play Store, one stands out thanks to its heart‑shaped icon featuring a Palestinian flag: “ Gaza Friendly ”. Created in June 2025, the label certifies shopkeepers involved in the boycott of products originating from the occupied Palestinian territories and marketed by companies supporting Israel ’s settlement expansion. To date, the app and its associated website list 80 businesses in France , mainly butchers, restaurants, bakeries, caterers, tea rooms and food distributors. The list is updated regularly, and the app features an interactive map allowing consumers to locate certified shops near their homes. The app, which has been downloaded more than 500 times so far, was created by Pierre-Amael Noailly Charny, a paediatrician of Tunisian origin from Lyon, in east-central France, along with a small group of friends. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Noailly Charny explains that shopkeepers who join Gaza Friendly can express their commitment to the Palestinian cause in a concrete way. ‘This label gives people outraged by the genocide in Gaza the possibility to turn their consumption into a lever for justice and solidarity’ - Pierre-Amael Noailly Charny, founder of Gaza Friendly “The existence of this label gives people outraged by the genocide in Gaza the possibility to turn their consumption into a lever for justice and solidarity,” Noailly Charny told Middle East Eye. The label draws inspiration from the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement, an international campaign launched in 2005 by Palestinian civil society to encourage consumers and institutions to refuse to buy Israeli products or goods originating from Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law. “Boycott works because refusing certain products cuts off resources from the oppression,” Gaza Friendly argues on its homepage, with the ambition of building a strong network of certified shopkeepers to give greater visibility to the boycott campaign. ‘My business is doing better’ To be certified, shopkeepers must comply with a three‑point charter: no Coca‑Cola Company beverages, no PepsiCo beverages, and no fresh products imported from Israeli settlements. For Noailly Charny, boycotting Coca‑Cola and PepsiCo is a peaceful tool with strong symbolic impact, given their documented involvement in the illegal occupation of Palestinian territories. In 2025, BDS revealed that Coca‑Cola operates a regional distribution centre and refrigerated warehouses in the settlement of Atarot in the West Bank, while PepsiCo is targeted for investments and subsidiaries linked to Israel. ‘The idea appealed to me, especially since some customers had already blamed me for selling Coca‑Cola’ - Akli, Gaza Friendly‑certified shopkeeper Although PepsiCo maintains it does not support Israel politically or militarily, activists argue that its ownership of Israeli brands SodaStream and Sabra, along with its operations in the country, amount to indirect support for the Israeli state. Coca‑Cola, for its part, insists that it does not endorse any country, government or policy, but has not addressed the allegations concerning the Atarot facility. Both companies declined to respond to MEE’s request for comment. “Even before Gaza Friendly existed, some shopkeepers had already taken the initiative to stop selling Coca‑Cola and Pepsi products. We therefore chose to put them in the spotlight and list them to set an example and encourage others to join,” Noailly Charny said. Aid Boucherie Halal in Creteil, near Paris, is one of the latest certified businesses. Its name appeared on the Gaza Friendly list on 4 September. Akli, the owner, says he heard about the label through an acquaintance. “The idea appealed to me, especially since some customers had already blamed me for selling Coca‑Cola. Personally, I didn’t know the company had interests in Israel,” he told MEE. Akli says he has always been supportive of Palestinians but didn’t know how to express that support. “Now I don’t sell Coca-Cola or Pepsi, and my business is doing just as well - actually, even better,” he said, noting a slight increase in customer numbers. Solidarity brands In addition to listing shopkeepers, Gaza Friendly provides them with visual materials such as posters and stickers to improve visibility. It also offers a non‑exhaustive list of alternative products, particularly beverages, to replace brands targeted by the boycott. Some of these drinks come from companies committed to Palestine. This is the case for Pales Drinks , a Belgian brand of sodas created in 2024 by young entrepreneur Abdelhakim Tarnach, which donates 10 percent of its profits to humanitarian actions in Palestine. Watermelon Index names and shames companies complicit in Israel's war on Gaza Read More » The same year saw the launch of Palestine Cola, a soft drink marketed by Safad Food AB, a company founded by entrepreneurs of Palestinian origin based in Malmo, Sweden. Here too, part of the profits from the sale of cans - decorated with an olive tree and wrapped in a keffiyeh pattern - funds emergency aid projects in Palestine such as clothing, tents and food assistance. In France, P alestine Cola is mainly distributed by Jebalia, an online retailer promoting alternative, ethical and solidarity‑based consumption. On its Instagram page , each purchase is presented as an act of support for humanitarian causes. Since July, Jebalia has been listed among Gaza Friendly‑certified businesses. Its owner Sofiane Slimani proudly embraces his commitment to Palestine. “We’ve reached a point where boycotting products linked to Israeli settlement activity is no longer enough. We need to offer alternatives,” he told MEE. Jebalia claims to have sold 100,000 cans of soda in 2025, its founding year. Beyond social media, the company uses other communication channels to make itself known. ‘We’ve reached a point where boycotting products linked to Israeli settlement activity is no longer enough. As olive harvest nears, Palestinian farmers urgently need international protection Submitted by Fareed Taamallah on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 14:23 Settlers armed and shielded by Israel are driving West Bank olive farmers off ancestral land. Sanctions on a handful of them will not stop the next attack Israeli military machinery uproots olive trees in the village of Beit Rima, near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, on 24 September 2026 (Reuters/Ali Sawafta) Off Every October, the ancient olive groves in my hometown and across the occupied West Bank become dynamic hubs of life and labour. For generations of Palestinians , the olive harvest has been the pulse of our economic survival and a living link to our ancestors. The olive tree, resilient and deep-rooted, is a symbol of who we are and of our connection to this land. As this year's harvest approaches, our villages are gripped by a dread I have not seen before. In recent weeks, the situation across the West Bank has deteriorated sharply. Military raids, arbitrary road closures and daily incursions by armed settler militias have turned our countryside into a militarised zone. This season is shaping up to be worse than any we have faced. With Israeli elections set for 27 October, political factions are openly competing over who can strike the most aggressive posture towards Palestinians. Settlers are better armed than ever, equipped with assault rifles and military gear, and backed by state institutions. Before a single olive has been picked, settler violence has already reached record levels, with the UN recording an average of more than six attacks a day in August. This terror hits close to home. In my village of Qira , in the Salfit governorate, my family and neighbours await the harvest with deep anxiety. Our ancestral groves, like those in surrounding villages, are targeted by the illegal settlements and outposts around them. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Harvesting our own trees, once an act of love and sustenance, has become a high-risk undertaking in which simply being present in the fields invites harassment, physical attack or expulsion. The political climate inside Israel has turned our groves into battlegrounds. Extremist settlers act with impunity because they know they have the structural backing of the state, the legal shield of military law and the direct protection of the Israeli army. State-backed militias To understand what is happening in Palestinian fields, one must first dismantle the false narrative that settler attacks are mere "vigilantism" or "friction" between civilians. Illegal Israeli settlers operate as a paramilitary arm of the Israeli state, carrying out ideological land grabs and violence with political cover and state sanction, often doing what the regular army cannot. Settlers are systematically armed, funded and protected by official institutions. Ministers in the Israeli government openly champion , finance and encourage settlement expansion and outpost construction. When armed settler militias descend on Palestinian groves in Qira or anywhere else in the West Bank, they are executing the state's broader policy of forcible transfer and territorial expansion. Across the West Bank, October 2025 alone saw 264 settler attacks, an average of 8.5 a day, making it the most violent month since OCHA began collecting data in 2006 When masked settlers attack farmers with iron rods, chainsaws and live ammunition, the military does not disarm or arrest them. Soldiers regularly stand guard, providing operational cover. If Palestinian villagers try to defend their families or protect their trees, the army turns its weapons on the victims, firing tear gas, rubber-coated steel bullets and live rounds at farmers. Settlers provide the physical violence required to push Palestinians off the land. The state provides the weapons, the political immunity and the legal mechanisms to seal off the newly seized territory. The scale of this campaign is documented in detail by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). During last year's harvest, OCHA recorded 178 harvest-related settler attacks across 88 Palestinian towns and villages, four times the number of communities affected in 2020. Across the West Bank, October 2025 alone saw 264 settler attacks, an average of 8.5 a day, making it the most violent month since OCHA began collecting data in 2006. More than 6,000 olive trees and saplings were vandalised over the year. Land dispossession This year is on course to be worse. According to the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, 49,000 olive trees were targeted in the first eight months of 2026, nearly double the figure for the same period last year. Around 100,000 West Bank families depend on olive income, and exports bring almost $200m into the Palestinian economy in a good year. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Beyond destroying trees, organised groups of settlers invade our groves to steal picked olives, confiscate harvesting tools, destroy storage sheds, cut irrigation pipes and vandalise vehicles. This violence works hand in hand with a bureaucratic system designed to strip us of our land through occupation law. The Israeli military routinely declares vast swathes of Palestinian farmland adjacent to settlements, outposts and settler-only bypass roads to be closed military zones, cutting off access overnight. Some 128,000 dunams of agricultural land have been inaccessible to their owners under permit restrictions since October 2023. Farmers are either barred from reaching their trees altogether or restricted to a one- or two-day window during the harvest under a "prior coordination" mechanism. Permission is often granted only after the olives have rotted on the branch or been stolen. Under military regulations and Ottoman-era property law co-opted by the Israeli Civil Administration, land declared "state land", or left uncultivated because farmers were blocked from reaching it, is confiscated. By using settler violence and military orders to physically prevent us from farming, the state creates the legal pretext it needs to absorb our groves into expanding settlement boundaries. We do not lack resilience or devotion to our soil. What we lack is basic physical protection. In Qira, as in hundreds of villages across the West Bank, unarmed families stand defenceless before state-backed paramilitary groups. To save our livelihoods and preserve our presence on our ancestral land, the international community must move from symbolic gestures to enforcement. Symbolic gestures In recent weeks, a group of western states, including the UK , France and Canada, has announced bans on trade with Israeli settlements and sanctions on individual extremist settlers and settlement-linked entities. These measures are a step in the right direction, but they fall drastically short of the scale of our reality. Sanctioning a handful of individuals ignores the state that arms and directs them. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); A trade ban on settlement products, or a visa ban on a few individuals, will not stop an armed group from descending on our groves in Qira tomorrow morning. These measures do not alter the calculus of a state that protects the aggressor and criminalises the victim. In defence of Israel's Jewish settlers in the West Bank Read More » As long as the political, military and economic architecture behind the settlement enterprise remains intact and unpunished, diplomatic statements will fail to protect a single olive tree or save a single farmer's life. We urgently call for an independent international protection force, or an expanded civilian observer presence, deployed directly to the agricultural zones most exposed to attack, including villages like Qira, throughout the West Bank during the olive harvest. Western governments must go further than partial measures and impose full arms embargoes, comprehensive sanctions and a complete boycott of the Israeli state institutions, military units, companies and financial entities that arm, direct or profit from settlement expansion and the infrastructure of occupation. The International Criminal Court, which has already issued arrest warrants for Israeli leaders over Gaza , must expedite its investigation into state-sponsored land theft, forced displacement and settler violence as war crimes and crimes against humanity. An olive tree takes decades to mature. A chainsaw or a canister of petrol in the hands of an armed settler can destroy centuries of heritage in seconds. Every unharvested olive and every burned tree is a deliberate attempt to force us off our land. As another harvest approaches under the shadow of state-sponsored violence, the world cannot afford to look away. We demand action, accountability and international protection before our land is emptied of its trees and its people.
