North Korea says test of intermediate-range strategic missile included use of AI. North Korea said it tested an intermediate-range strategic missile on Saturday that involved the use of AI, hours after Seoul said Pyongyang had launched a ballistic missile. The launch took place days after Seoul’s military demanded an apology from Pyongyang for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that it blamed on the North. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month’s explosion and called South Korea “despicable” on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul’s civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue. Early on Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan. “South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defence posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometres. Hours later, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Pyongyang’s leader Kim Jong Un, said the missile fired in the morning was an “intermediate-range strategic missile”. She said the projectile is “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it”, without elaborating further on the use of artificial intelligence. She said it meant “there is no way to avoid” the missile’s attack, and claimed Kim Jong Un believed “any country in the world could not have access to such technology for at least several years”. Her latest statement followed Kim Jong Un’s remarks last month stressing the need to raise “the level of artificial intelligence” in the country’s weapons systems. Kim Yo Jong claimed that whenever North Korea “applied the wave-like trajectory mode”, South Korea “failed to track the targets from their first skip points”. Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile technology with Russian military support in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine. “AI is increasingly being incorporated into military technology worldwide, and ballistic missiles are no exception,” Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs, told AFP . “AI can assist with target information and launch operations, while the wars in Ukraine and Iran have shown how linking AI with drones and missiles can enhance their operational effectiveness.” Hong said it was too early to conclude North Korea’s claims about the missile’s capabilities were accurate. “North Korea’s missile technology is not particularly advanced compared with leading military powers,” he said. “While missiles that manoeuvre in their terminal phase are difficult to intercept, that does not mean they can strike their targets with perfect accuracy.” ‘Despicable’ Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month’s explosion inside the DMZ was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border. North Korea’s military has placed mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un’s designation of South Korea as his country’s “ principal enemy ” in 2024. The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work, according to South Korea’s defence minister Kang Shin-chul. South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo Jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts. She ridiculed Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch” and said the military’s demand that her country apologise was “quite ridiculous”. Kim also warned Pyongyang was “ready for everything” Seoul might do over the mine blast — remarks followed the next morning by Pyongyang’s missile launch. Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government’s diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement. “Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP . “The message is that the North is pursuing … confrontation in response to goodwill.”

Indian police detain several people in Gen Z-led protests against voter roll changes. Indian police detained several people in New Delhi on Saturday, disrupting a second day of protests backed by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party and other opposition groups against changes to voter rolls. The protesters say the changes benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s governing party and are demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. The demonstrations mark the latest in a series of youth-led protests that have emerged this year, putting pressure on Modi unprecedented in his 12 years in power. About 100 demonstrators removed security barricades on Saturday and chanted “vote thief, leave the post” and “Gyanesh Kumar, step down” before police forcibly detained some of them. Independent lawmaker Kapil Sibal, left-wing All India Students’ Association President Neha Bora and political activists Prashant Bhushan and Yogendra Yadav were among the protesters, according to a Reuters witness. The police declined to comment on the number and identity of those detained. “First they removed people from the voters list and now they are not letting us raise our voice against this. This is not acceptable,” Bora told Reuters . Neha Bora, National President of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), is detained by police during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India on October 3, 2026. — Reuters The chief of the Election Commission, Kumar, has not commented on the protests and the demands to step down. On Friday, police stopped a group of protesters from gathering, bundling them into buses. Several nearby metro stations remained shut amid tight security. Though police released many of those detained on Friday, they charged several of them with allegedly violating orders banning mass gatherings in Delhi, according to a police source. Critics say a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls. The commission, long regarded as one of the country’s most trusted institutions, says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters. On Friday, the commission directed officials to register newly eligible voters and those omitted from electoral rolls.

Lahore magistrate sends female suspect to jail on judicial remand in Azeri woman's rape case. LAHORE: A judicial magistrate on Saturday sent a woman suspect to jail on a 14-day judicial remand in connection with a case of an Azeri woman’s rape. The 20-year-old Azerbaijan national had travelled to Pakistan for business purposes and was allegedly gang-raped by three men in a rented flat of a private housing society near Raiwind on the night between Sept 25 and Sept 26. Two of those men had been arrested and were sent on a six-day physical remand on Tuesday. In her statement , the complainant had named two women with whom she had met before the men accused of raping her gathered with them at an apartment. One woman had secured pre-arrest bail while the other was arrested and sent on a three-day physical remand on Wednesday. On Saturday, upon the completion of her remand, the police produced the woman suspect before Magistrate Azhar Mahmood. The investigating officer told the magistrate that as further custody of the suspect was not required for investigation, she could be sent to jail on judicial remand. Subsequently, the magistrate allowed the request and sent the suspect on a 14-day judicial remand until Oct 17. Meanwhile, Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Investigation Syed Zeeshan Raza noted that a total of three suspects have been arrested so far, while one was still at large. Addressing a press conference, the DIG said swabs of the survivor and the suspects were taken and sent to the forensic science agency for further investigation. The ages of the suspects were between 25 and 30 years. He also claimed that the suspects had confessed to their crime and police were continuing their investigation. DIG Raza said the suspects had threatened the woman for having contacts with influential people and stopped her from approaching the police. Survivor’s statement The Defence C police had registered a first information report (FIR) against three unidentified suspects on September 26 on the Azeri woman’s complaint. In her statement under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) , the survivor said she had arrived in Islamabad from Istanbul on Sept 13 and stayed in Faisalabad for five days before travelling to Lahore. “I had a plan to visit Skardu, but I could not go there because I was alone,” she said. According to her, on the day of the alleged incident, she messaged two women, asking them to meet her in Lahore. At around 11pm, she went to a cafe where she met one of them — the woman sent on remand today — and later accompanied her to a house in Bahria Town to meet the other, who has secured pre-arrest bail until Oct 5 . The complainant told the magistrate that at around 2am, a white car arrived carrying two men, one of whom was sent on remand on Tuesday (first suspect). Later, they moved to an apartment where two more men arrived, one of whom was the second person sent on remand (second suspect), while she did not know the name of the other man. According to the complainant, in a separate room, the woman on bail took between Rs20,000 and Rs30,000 from the first suspect, saying the money was for a party, while the woman now on remand also joined them. The Azeri woman said she made it clear that she “did not need money or alcohol”. She alleged that the first suspect tried to touch her and locked her in a separate room. When she asked about her friends, she was told that they had left. When she tried to leave, the complainant said she was told that she could not go because her friends had taken money. The victim said she offered to pay the men, but they told her that she would have to drink alcohol with them before they would let her go. She alleged that the three men raped her. She further stated that the suspects then put her in a car and threw her out at an unknown location, while threatening her with dire consequences if she approached the police. According to her statement, the suspects also took her handbag containing Rs200,000, an iPhone 13 Pro Max and another mobile phone. She then requested some people present there to help her call the police emergency number 15, following which the police arrived. It is the second such case in which a foreign woman was reportedly gang-raped in the Defence C police station area during the last four months. In June, two foreign women, nationals of the Netherlands and Venezuela, were allegedly abducted and sexually assaulted in the Defence C police station area. According to the FIR, the women were abducted by five suspects, including a close relative of a senior political personality, who demanded ransom and subjected them to sexual assault during their captivity.

Fatima Sana joins Perth Scorchers for Women’s Big Bash League. Pakistan women’s cricket captain Fatima Sana has signed a one-year contract with Perth Scorchers for the upcoming Women’s Big Bash League (WBBL) season, the Australian club announced on Saturday. The 24-year-old all-rounder will be available for the Scorchers’ first eight matches of WBBL 12, which begins on Oct 29. Her stay could be extended if she receives permission from the Pakistan Cricket Board to miss a training camp ahead of the national side’s expected tour of the West Indies in December. Fatima becomes only the second Pakistani player to feature in the WBBL, following former captain Nida Dar, who represented Sydney Thunder in 11 matches during the 2019 edition. The signing marks Fatima’s WBBL debut and her second overseas T20 league appearance this year, having played for Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred . “I’ve watched the WBBL from Pakistan and always wondered what it would feel like to be part of this great competition,” Fatima said in a statement issued by the Scorchers. “To now wear the Scorchers colours, represent such a great club and walk out at the WACA Ground in front of members and fans, while being cheered on by people back home, is incredibly special. This really is a dream come true.” A right-arm medium-fast bowler and middle-order batter, Fatima made her international debut in 2019 and has since established herself as one of Pakistan’s leading all-rounders. She has represented Pakistan in more than 130 white-ball matches. Earlier this year, she set a record for the fastest half-century in women’s T20 internationals when she reached the landmark in 15 balls against Zimbabwe. Perth Scorchers general manager Kade Harvey welcomed Fatima’s signing, describing her as “one of the most exciting young allrounders in world cricket”. He said the club was looking forward to seeing her perform at the WACA Ground.

Efforts underway to repatriate remains of 3 Pakistanis killed while recovering hijacked tanker from Somali pirates: PMO. The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) on Saturday said that arrangements were underway to repatriate the remains of three Pakistani sailors, who were killed during an operation earlier this week to recover a hijacked oil tanker off the coast of Somalia. The maritime police force of Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland said on Tuesday that it had recovered the MT Honour 25 , a Palau-flagged oil tanker with 19 crew members on board, including 10 Pakistanis. The Foreign Office confirmed on Wednesday that three Pakistanis had died and three others were injured during the operation, later identifying the deceased as Rafiullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmed Ansari. According to a statement by the PMO issued on Saturday, arrangements were being made to repatriate the sailors’ remains as per the instructions of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The remains had been taken to Ethiopia’s capital Addis Ababa, with Ethiopian Airlines reviewing the next steps for transferring the bodies. “Following this, final approval will be granted for their departure on a flight bound for Karachi. In accordance with the prime minister’s instructions, the relevant authorities are in continuous contact to expedite the repatriation process,” the statement read. It added that the premier had assured of “all possible assistance” in bringing the deceased sailors home. PM Shehbaz has announced a relief package worth Rs12.5 million for the deceased sailors’ families, the PMO said yesterday. The prime minister announced financial support for the families of the deceased, including free housing and free education for their children. The PMO added that the premier spoke with Syed Kashif Umer’s son, Azhan Kashif, on the phone to extend his condolences and express his grief. Yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said that four of the 10 Pakistani crew members had been “safely retrieved” and were scheduled to arrive in Karachi today. The four crew members — Yasir Khan, Aqeel Khan, Amin bin Shams and Usman Ghani — were retrieved following “sustained efforts” by FO and Pakistan’s embassy in Djibouti, Dar said. Months with no progress The MT Honour 25 had been hijacked by Somali pirates on April 21, around 30 nautical miles off Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland region. Apart from Pakistanis, the vessel’s crew also included seven Indonesians, an Indian and a Sri Lankan. For around five months, there had been no progress either in negotiations or in the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages, despite concerns abounding about their declining health. Since the hijacking, the crew made several emotional videos and audio appeals , reporting that they ran out of clean water, food and medicine. For its part, FO maintained that it remained “actively engaged” to secure the release of the sailors. On Sept 29, Somali maritime police recovered the Palau-flagged oil tanker amid reports of casualties among the crew. “The naval and ground units of the Puntland Maritime Police Force conducted a planned operation in the Dharin-Bar area of Bandar Beyla district,” the maritime police had said in its initial statement. In another statement, it announced that the operation had concluded and the recovered vessel was “now safe and under the Puntland government’s control”. During the operation, it said, 21 suspected pirates were apprehended, while operations to locate the remaining members continue. “Before the operation [had] begun, the pirates on board the ship killed five of the crew. Among those killed were three from Pakistan, one from Myanmar and one from India,” it said.

Trump shares Republican senator's phone number in feud over daylight saving bill. US President Donald Trump on Saturday posted the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator online, escalating a feud over daylight saving time. Trump’s post on Truth Social urged people to call a phone number that he said belonged to Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican. The dispute centres on the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent and end the twice-yearly practice of changing clocks by one hour. Trump says most Americans want more afternoon sunlight, but Cotton has argued the change would plunge early risers into darkness during winter months. “Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important bill,” Trump wrote. When Reuters called the Arkansas number, it went directly to a voicemail box that did not identify itself as belonging to Cotton. It’s the president’s second posting in as many days about Cotton’s opposition to the bill. “Nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning clocks back twice a year and having sunshine in the afternoon is better than early in the morning!” Trump wrote. Most US states have observed the time switch since the 1960s. Clocks this year are slated to switch back to standard time on November 1. In a Senate speech last October, Cotton said he would “always oppose” making daylight saving time permanent, adding that it would “again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans”. The US House of Representatives passed the bill in July, but Cotton is not alone in the Senate. Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, this week called the bill “dead as disco” and said he did not think that Senate Majority Leader John Thune would bring the measure for a vote. The offices of Cotton and Thune did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday. Golfers, farmers cited as supporters The first constituency that Trump cited as wanting the change was golfers. The president shared an October 1 letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp supporting the bill. “The PGA Tour, as an example, needs more daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments,” said Trump, who often spends weekends at his golf clubs around the country. He also pointed to tennis players, hunters and farmers as proponents of year-round daylight saving time. This is not the first time Trump has shared a senator’s phone number to make a point. During his first presidential campaign in 2015, Trump read Senator Lindsey Graham’s phone number at a rally and dismissed the South Carolina Republican as an “idiot”. They later reconciled, with the late Graham becoming one of Trump’s highest-profile allies in Congress. The intra-party dispute comes as Trump campaigns for Republicans across the country, including in Ohio on Saturday. Cotton is running for re-election, but his race is not considered competitive, as Trump received more than 64 per cent of the Arkansas vote in the 2024 presidential election.

Local automakers voice concerns as imports of used cars surge in Sept. ISLAMABAD: Imports of used cars surged in September after easing of regulations, inviting criticism from local manufacturers while importers claim that the move will bring competition in the auto sector. After a brief decline due to the government abolishing the Pers­onal Baggage Scheme and applying restrictions to control misuse of used car schemes for overseas Pakistanis, imports of used cars have started surging again. In the month of September, a total of 2,276 vehicles were imported under the Gift Scheme as the strict restrictions under the Baggage Scheme continue, according to data from the Commerce Ministry. The figures show that in May, only 48 used cars were imported mainly through the baggage scheme. However, the situation started to change from June onwards. In June, a total of 843 vehicles were imported, including 806 under the Gift Scheme. The figure reached 1,938 in July, with 1,876 cars under the Gift Scheme. August saw a total of 1,445 vehicle imports, while 2,276 vehicles were imported in September, with 2,238 under the Gift Scheme. A senior executive of the auto industry noted that the reduction in duties on completely built units (CBUs) by 20-25 per cent in the 2026-27 budget has reduced the import cost. “We have reports that a one-year restriction on transfer of ownership is not being implemented in some cities, due to which this business is flourishing again, but at the cost of the domestic auto industry which consists of 13 assemblers and over 300 auto parts manufacturers,” the executive added. Auto parts vendors expressed their concerns too, claiming that auto production had finally begun to show an increase after a gap of three years, which was also contributing to Pakistan’s growth in the large-scale manufacturing (LSM) sector . “Locally produced cars contain up to 60pc local parts by value, amounting to an average of Rs1.5 million per vehicle, and import of 2,276 used vehicles meant loss of Rs3.4 billion of local parts production which creates jobs and operates in the documented economy,” said Abdul Rehman Aizaz, chairman of Pakistan Asso­ciation of Automotive Parts and Ac­­cessories Manufacturers (Paa­pam). He termed it unfair that, on the one hand, the proposed auto policy was slashing import duties on new cars, while on the other hand, imports of used cars were being encouraged. “Ultimately, Pakistan is moving towards a market dominated by imported new and used vehicles with no industrial activity,” the Paapam chairman said, terming the business of used cars completely unregulated. Competition in auto sector On the contrary, importers claim that Pakistan needs to have a competitive economy and that importing used cars was completely legal if done as per the government regulations. “Currently, all imported vehicles are subjected to pre-shipment inspections by the accredited companies based in Japan as most of the used cars are imported from that country,” said Mian Shaoib Ahmed, chairman of All Pakistan Car Dealers & Importers Association. Ahmed, also a member of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce & Industry’s (FPCCI) executive committee, stressed there was a demand for used cars in Pakistan. He contended that new Chinese entrants have yet to make their mark in Pakistani markets, while Japanese car assemblers in the country were not yet ready for the competitive environment. The FPCCI member lauded the government for recent changes in the vehicle import regime and added that used car imports under the Gift Scheme and commercial imports will continue to rise in the coming months. Ahmed referred to a notification by the Engineering Development Board (EDB), dated Sep 30, which would relax the criteria for imports of used vehicles. The changes in the recent EDB notification against the earlier notification included the removal of a clause for the minimum capital requirement of a company importing used cars, and now, any tax-registered individual or firm not even registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) can import vehicles. The pre- and post-shipment inspection will be conducted through the Pakistan Standards and Quality Control Authority (PSQCA) instead of the EDB. However, the PSQCA chief executive officer said that inspection was not done directly under or by the authority, but through its registered inspection agencies. Currently, only two local inspection agents have been registered with the PSQCA; they are the representatives of firms accredited with the Japanese Foreign Principals Inspection Agencies.

Pakistan summons Indian envoy over killing of 2 civilians by border troops. Pakistan summoned the Indian chargé d’affaires to lodge a strong protest over the killing of two Pakistani civilians by Indian Border Security Force (BSF) personnel in the Bedian sector along the international border, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday. Two unarmed Pakistani civilians were martyred and another was injured in firing by India’s BSF near the border in Kasur on Friday. “The BSF personnel resorted to unprovoked and lethal force against unarmed civilians. Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives,” the FO said. Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterise the deceased as “infiltrators”, it added. The FO said the incident constituted a serious violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life, and raised concerns over the protection of civilian life under international law. It called on the Indian side to “conduct an immediate, transparent and credible investigation”, take appropriate disciplinary and legal action against those responsible, and formally communicate the findings and action taken to the government of Pakistan. India was further urged to “respect fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in such situations, and take effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future”, the FO said. Across the border, India’s foreign ministry said it had summoned the chargé d’affaires of the Pakistan High Commission to protest what it alleged was the “continued facilitation of illegal cross-border infiltration from Pakistan”. The three civilians were residents of Ladhar village and had moved a few steps ahead of a border pillar when the BSF opened fire on them without warning. All three were unarmed. The deceased were identified as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt, both residents of Jattan Wali Haveli, Ladhar. The injured civilian was taken for medical treatment. According to security sources, none of the three men had attempted to cross the border fence, with the incident described as a violation of the border agreement and standard operating procedures governing the international border. The development comes a day after Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry lampooned India’s claims of “neutralising” a “terrorist” allegedly linked to the Pakistani military, presenting the individual during a press conference. Asked whether the recent allegations could trigger another armed conflict between the neighbours during the press briefing, he affirmed that Pakistan’s armed forces were always ready for any such move and warned of “very harsh” retribution. Additional input from Reuters

UAE investigators say flydubai co-pilot was planning 'terrorist act'. The United Arab Emirates’ attorney general said the co-pilot of a flydubai flight to Israel had planned a “terrorist act” and used the cockpit’s emergency axe to attack the captain, the official UAE news agency WAM reported on Saturday. The news agency quoted Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying that according to the initial findings of an investigation , “the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act” and had “attacked the captain in the cockpit with the emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft”. Separately, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had earlier showered the Indian captain with praise for saving the plane, invited him to Israel as a guest of honour. “You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world,” Netanyahu said in a video his office released of his telephone conversation with Captain Smit Machchhar. UAE Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, also the country’s defence minister and the crown prince of Dubai, visited Smit at a hospital. In a post on X, he described him as the “pilot who embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life”. The defence minister added: “From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. “We are proud that he is part of our team… part of the story of our nation… and part of what the UAE stands for… a nation of compassion… a nation of peace… and a nation of life.” Barred from flying The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a flydubai flight to Israel had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views, multiple media outlets reported. Scrutiny into the alleged assailant — who was identified in the reports as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami — and his motives has intensified after Wednesday’s drama aboard a Dubai-Tel Aviv route that officials say narrowly avoided catastrophe. During the flydubai flight, the jet’s Indian captain was assaulted by his co-pilot but he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Omani authorities had banned the pilot from flying over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views, citing people familiar with the matter. CNN , citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year over concerns about extremist views. Al Arabiya , citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views. The broadcaster said he had also spent time in Syria, raising concerns he may have been influenced by radical groups there. ABC News , citing senior intelligence and law enforcement officials familiar with the investigation, reported the suspect had allegedly been found in possession of extremist materials while he was a trainee.

Tennessee prison chief who oversaw botched execution resigns: governor. The prison commissioner in the southern US state of Tennessee has resigned over the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike, Governor Bill Lee said on Saturday. Lee said in a statement that commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post this month. Pike’s lawyers say she is in critical condition, unconscious and on a ventilator in a hospital, after her execution by lethal injection went wrong on Wednesday. Pike, 50, survived two injections of the normally lethal substance pentobarbital as punishment for the murder of Colleen Slemmer in 1995. It was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year. The state halted an execution in May after medical staff failed to tap a vein in the prisoner’s arm. Lee said he thanked Strada for “his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment”. In the same statement, Strada said, “I continue to believe the Department (of Correction) carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol.” Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, has halted further executions through the rest of the year while a review is conducted. Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries. In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.

Bilawal says Centre was ready to impose emergency in KP but PPP sought 'political solution'. PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Saturday said the federal government had made up its mind to impose emergency or governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; however, his party suggested finding a political solution to fight terrorism in a “better way”. Addressing an event in Karachi, Bilawal said that the federal government had been in contact with President Asif Ali Zardari and the PPP regarding the recent security situation, particularly in KP. Noting the terrorist attacks emanating from Afghanistan, Bilawal said, “In my opinion, the federal government had made up its mind and was 100 per cent ready; they wanted to immediately impose emergency or governor’s rule in KP.” He noted that although imposing governor’s rule or emergency in any province was a Constitutional tool, the PPP “was of the view that before dropping this constitutional atomic bomb, political parties should absolutely find a political solution to fight terrorism in a better way”. Sharing his party’s view, Bilawal said the PPP wanted to hold talks with the protesting party — the PTI — regarding its planned Oct 4 long march to Islamabad before making any decision. While calling on all parties to engage in dialogue with PTI before imposing emergency, he also urged the latter to abandon its long march to Islamabad and acknowledge the success of their protest. Onus on state to protect kids from online harm, IHC told. • NCRC recommends boosting NCCIA capacity, setting up special units for exploitation probes • Proposes Peca review from child rights perspective • Urges integrating age verification into Digital Nation Pakistan Act ISLAMABAD: Protecting minors from online grooming, exploitation and harmful content is the state’s responsibility, the National Commission on the Rights of Child (NCRC) told the Islamabad High Court while proposing sweeping legal and institutional reforms to safeguard children on social media. In a 17-page response submitted to the court in a case concerning social media usage by children under the age of 16, the commission acknowledged the concerns raised in the petition. It underscored the need for age verification mechanisms and a comprehensive regulatory framework, stating that effective legal and regulatory measures are indispensable for online child safety. The NCRC recommended integrating child online safety into the regulatory framework of the Digital Nation Pakistan Act, with a focus on age verification and effective protection systems. To combat technology-facilitated child exploitation, the commission recommended boosting the capacity of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency and establishing specialised systems to investigate online child sexual exploitation. The commission also recommended a review and amendment of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in the context of child rights, noting the need to improve the existing legal framework for online child safety. Digital platforms must be made more accountable for child safety, the commission said. It urged effective action against child sexual abuse material and online grooming, while implementing measures for the immediate removal of such content. “There is also a need to limit unnecessary online contact between children and unknown adults,” the commission said, adding that legislation, platform accountability and effective enforcement are essential for children’s online safety. The NCRC noted the importance of striking an effective balance between children’s digital rights and their protection online. The commission asserted that the issue of children’s online safety demands effective legal and institutional measures rather than mere policy. Advocates Muhammad Jalal Haider and Yahya Farid are representing the petitioner in the case. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE MAKING OF HAMAS. During the 1970s and 1980s, a dramatic political shift permanently altered the geopolitical topography of the Middle East and the broader Muslim world. Islamism gained momentum as secular nationalism declined. It was a collapse accelerated by the defeat of Egypt, Syria and Jordan in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War. At the time, Western powers viewed Islamism, a right-wing ideology opposed to socialism and secular nationalism, as a useful counterweight to Soviet-backed nationalist regimes in Egypt, Syria, Iraq and, later, Libya. One of the most consequential applications of this strategy unfolded in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Gaza. Anti-Israel Palestinian resistance was largely dominated by secular and left-leaning groups operating primarily within the Israeli-occupied territories of Palestine and neighbouring nationalist Arab states. The French scholar Jean-Pierre Filiu wrote that, in order to neutralise Palestinian resistance groups, Israel quietly nurtured the growth of local Islamist movements, specifically the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood. This was a deliberate strategy, designed to fragment and undermine the primary face of Palestinian nationalism: Yasser Arafat’s left-leaning and secular Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO). For Israeli strategists, the PLO’s anti-colonial rhetoric posed a serious political threat. To curb the PLO’s influence, Israeli military intelligence began to cultivate a counterweight in the shape of Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. A charismatic Palestinian cleric, Yassin had begun building a social and religious network under the Muslim Brotherhood umbrella in Gaza, culminating in the founding of al-Mujama al-Islami in 1973. The PLO viewed Yassin’s followers as “quietist fundamentalists” preoccupied with social welfare and moral purification. The PLO did not exhibit concern even when Israeli authorities permitted al-Mujama to operate unhindered. In 1979, the Israeli military administration formally recognised the al-Mujama charity, granting it permission to establish mosques, schools and medical clinics across Gaza. Israel’s relentless efforts, across decades, to weaken secular Palestinian resistance to its occupation of Palestine by backing a ‘counterweight’ ultimately backfired. The current Hamas is the blowback According to Filiu, while PLO sympathisers faced relentless crackdowns, Yassin was allowed to build a vast social network. Gulf funds, primarily from Saudi Arabia, flowed into al-Mujama’s coffers with minimal Israeli interference. In 1978, Israeli authorities even permitted the establishment of an Islamic university in Gaza, which eventually became a stronghold for Islamist recruitment. Years later, Brig Gen Yitzhak Segev, the Israeli military governor of Gaza in the late 1970s and early 1980s, admitted that he was provided a state budget to assist in funding Yassin’s project to offset the PLO. In the book Israel’s Wars, political scientist Ahron Bregman wrote that defence minister Yitzhak Rabin maintained a policy throughout the 1980s of tolerating Yassin and his organisation’s activities, provided their hostility remained directed at the PLO rather than Israeli soldiers. Illustration by Abro The late 1970s and early 1980s saw violent clashes erupt across Gaza and the West Bank between the PLO and Yassin’s followers. Members and supporters of al-Mujama torched PLO offices, attacked cinemas and targeted secular intellectuals. However, the assumption that Yassin’s movement would remain a benign social organisation focused solely on rivalling the PLO proved to be a miscalculation. Writing in The Wall Street Journal in 2009, journalist Andrew Higgins documented how Israeli forces raided Yassin’s home in 1984 following a tip-off, discovering a concealed weapons cache. Yassin was arrested and sentenced to 12 years in prison. Yet, Higgins added, in a move underscoring Israel’s persistent conviction that Islamists remained a secondary threat compared to secular nationalists, Israel released Yassin just 11 months later, in 1985. The turning point occurred in December 1987 with the outbreak of the first Intifada, a spontaneous grassroots uprising against Israeli occupation. Fearing that the PLO would bounce back to take command of the uprising, Yassin and his inner circle transformed al-Mujama al-Islami into a militant resistance organisation. In early 1988, the group published its founding covenant under a new name: Hamas. Hamas was thus the direct byproduct of a charitable and proselytising network shaped in the 1970s by the Gaza chapter of the Muslim Brotherhood and facilitated by Israeli policy. Its original objective of drawing Palestinians toward religious piety and discrediting secular groups, evolved during the Intifada into an armed struggle. Hamas’ 1988 charter combined militant anti-Zionism with unyielding Islamism, calling for an Islamic state in Palestine and rejecting the PLO’s gradual move toward a diplomatic, two-state compromise. Even during the initial months of the Intifada, Israeli authorities hesitated to suppress Hamas with the severity applied to the PLO, hoping the group would fracture the uprising. However, as Higgins observed, when Hamas initiated armed attacks, kidnappings and suicide operations against Israeli personnel, Tel Aviv recognised the scale of its strategic error. By the time Israel outlawed Hamas and rearrested Yassin in 1989, the network that Israel helped nurture was deeply entrenched. This manoeuvre yielded a fierce adversary. Much like the American backing of the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s, Israel’s policy towards the Palestinian Muslim Brotherhood became a classic instance of strategic blowback. A quietist religious charity group transformed into an entrenched militant movement. Even after the PLO’s influence waned from the 1990s onwards, evidence indicates that Israel’s strategic interest in leveraging Hamas persisted. As reported by The New York Times and The Times of Israel in 2023, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition governments facilitated hundreds of millions of dollars in Qatari cash transfers into Gaza between 2009 and 2023. The objective was to keep Hamas viable in Gaza, thereby keeping the Palestinian leadership permanently divided and isolating the PLO in the West Bank. Netanyahu explicitly articulated this doctrine during his party’s meeting in March 2019, stating: “Anyone who wants to thwart the establishment of a Palestinian state has to support bolstering Hamas…” This was widely quoted by major Israeli newspapers. This policy relied on tactical coordination, work-permit allocations and economic incentives to manage Hamas, while derailing two-state diplomatic efforts. As detailed in one of Israel’s largest newspapers, Haaretz, in 2023, this long-standing gamble to sustain Hamas as a political wedge ultimately collapsed with the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the aftermath, some analysts argued that the far-right Israeli administration intentionally overlooked intelligence warnings to allow an attack that could serve as a pretext for destroying Gaza and dismantling opposition in the West Bank. In November 2023, The New York Times reporters Ronen Bergman and Adam Goldman revealed that Israeli military and intelligence agencies had possessed a detailed, 40-page Hamas attack plan for over a year. This may be a show of reckless indifference, or an exhibition of hubris and a flawed strategic doctrine that assumed Hamas was permanently deterred. Indeed, but there is an increasing number of analysts who view the failure to act on these blueprints as evidence of deliberate omission. Published in Dawn, EOS, October 4th, 2026

After hours of negotiations, second round of govt-opposition talks ends in a 'deadlock'. The meeting at Parliament House began after 4pm on Saturday, with discussions focusing on the PTI’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad. Details on the negotiating process were sparse as both sides seemingly agreed not to speak to the media before matters concluded. However, shortly before 3am on Sunday, Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, who was part of the opposition delegation, told the media that the talks had not succeeded in a breakthrough. “Deadlock,” he told reporters waiting at Parliament House in footage aired on Geo News . Asked what the points of contention were, he said they were “small things”. He added that the “issue” of meetings with PTI founder Imran Khan could not be solved. He went on to say that the deadlock was over Imran’s meeting with his personal physicians, and how to address terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He said that talks had now ended, adding that a detailed press conference would be held later. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, who was part of the government’s delegation in the talks, said the talks failed primarily because the “KP government could not assure whether they would cooperate in the fight against terrorism in the future”. He alleged that the PTI’s provincial government in KP did not want to implement the National Action Plan and that the PTI delegation that participated in the talks had also left the venue “disappointed because the KP government did not cooperate on terrorism”. An agreement had been reached on all other matters, he said in response to a question. Asked about the possible future course of action, he said the “Constitution has several options”, seemingly a referring to the possibility of imposing governor’s rule or emergency in KP. Separately, PPP’s Sherry Rehman, who also participated in the talks, said the government delegation debated all points with the opposition. “Unfortunately, the draft [agreement] was changed four times after it was agreed upon,” she told Geo News , adding that she would not go into the details. At the same time, he asserted that imposing an emergency or governor rule was not the answer to the protest. He further said that the participants had also not reached an agreement on when the next round of talks would take place. He said that the opposition’s demands presented during the second round of talks were “simple” and included meetings with Imran and his spouse, Bushra Bibi. He said that there were a few issues pertaining to terrorism, where the negotiating process became “stuck”. Tariq Fazal objects to KP CM’s remarks CM Afridi’s Saturday statement vowed to hold the long march on Oct 4 and to prevent a repeat of the events of May 9, 2023. A source privy to the huddle told Dawn the emergency option was discussed, but participants agreed to first give the opposition a chance to settle matters peacefully through dialogue, and to seriously consider an emergency only if the PTI did not back down. The coalition also believes the march will remain confined to KP and not enter Punjab or Islamabad. On Thursday, Sanaullah said the government and PTI were engaged in “off-the-record talks” over the protest, and that the decision on the march rested with the PTI’s senior leadership, “with whom off-the-record consultation is ongoing”. “So let us see, even if they do not postpone it, we have arrangements in place to stop them,” he warned. FAO flags gaps in Pakistan’s nutritious food supply. • UN agency says over 60pc of citizens unable to afford healthy diet • Calls for overhaul of agrifood system ISLAMABAD: The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations has emphasised the urgent need to transform Pakistan’s agrifood system to improve access to healthy diets, a critical step towards addressing all forms of malnutrition and their related costs to society. The UN agency, in its latest assessment on “Food Supply for Healthy Diets in Pakistan”, observed that a major challenge in the country’s current food supply is the persistent mismatch between the quantities of food available and those required for the population to consume a healthy diet aligned with the national food-based dietary guidelines (FBDGs). “Enabling access to healthy diets for all is essential to achieving Pakistan’s national development priorities. Yet over 60 per cent of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet, contributing to the high rates of malnutrition across the country. At the same time, diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCD) are rising, while various forms of undernutrition persist. Unhealthy diets are a common cause of all forms of malnutrition and contribute directly to morbidity and mortality from NCD,” the assessment shows. The FAO listed priority policy actions to strengthen demand for healthy diets through consumer-focused policies; updating Pakistan’s FBDGs to reflect nutrition, health, and environmental priorities and use it for nutrition education and behavior change; introducing evidence-based fiscal measures, including taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages and other foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats; introducing front-of-pack nutrition labelling to help consumers make informed food choices; protecting vulnerable populations; restricting the marketing of unhealthy foods, particularly those targeting children, expanding nutritious school meal programmes; and strengthening social protection programmes to improve access to nutritious foods. The assessment recommended reorienting the agrifood system to deliver healthy diets, aligning agricultural policies and investment priorities to increase support for the production of vegetables, fruits, pulses, roots and tubers across the country, while supporting milk production in some regions; and providing greater incentives for food processors to meet food safety and quality standards and reformulate foods to reduce salt, sugar and unhealthy fats. It called for promoting healthier retail food environments, through investments in storage, cold chains, and market infrastructure to reduce losses. These actions, combined with regular monitoring, can contri­bute to increasing access to and consumption of healthy diets in Paki­stan, both today and in the future. The FAO assessment says large gaps were observed for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, and legumes and pulses. However, important misalignment exists between Pakistan’s dietary guidelines and food supply, with supply gaps for several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, legumes and pulses, while the supply for staples and sugar exceeds what is needed for healthy diets. “Enabling equitable access to diverse, nutritious, safe, and affordable foods that support healthy diets is a policy imperative for Pakistan,” the assessment said. Tight monetary policy likely to continue. KARACHI: As the world continues to grapple with uncertain oil prices, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) is unlikely to meet its FY27 mid-term inflation target of 5-7 per cent, financial experts and analysts said. Consumer Price Index-based inflation of 10.3 per cent in September clearly indicates that industry, businesses, and the general public will bear the brunt of these cost-push inflationary pressures. Experts believe the central bank will not lower interest rates to stimulate economic activity. Instead, it will maintain a tight monetary stance to support ‘sustainable’ growth. For the past four years, the government and the SBP have been satisfied with low but sustainable growth of around 3 to 3.7 per cent—a level that creates no jobs and does not address the severe problem of 44 per cent of Pakistanis living in poverty. “There is no domestic or foreign investment, and existing industries are struggling to survive. The situation would not change unless a comprehensive economic policy is introduced to support domestic investment, which is being undermined by inflated energy prices and overall double-digit inflation,” said Amir Aziz, a manufacturer and exporter of textile made-ups. “Inflation is only one factor. Bangladesh is in a much better position, as energy costs about 7 to 8 cents per unit, compared with 14 to 16 cents in Pakistan. This gives Bangladesh an advantage over Pakistani products,” said Mr Mohammad Hasham, who recently returned home after serving the Bangladesh textile industry for 25 years as the head of some of its largest textile units. He said double-digit inflation is killing both the industry and investors, and economic activity is slowing, causing pain for the general public. Tresmark Chief Executive Faisal Mamsa said that Pakistan’s authorities reportedly expect inflation to average around 7.5pc if oil returns towards $80, and around 8.2pc if it remains near $100 per barrel. “They also expect inflation to moderate after December and argue that the current 11.5pc policy rate remains appropriate,” he said. However, many experts disagree that the SBP policy rate will remain unchanged at 11.5pc despite double-digit inflation. At the same time, the government raised cut-off yields by up to 75 basis points, with the highest at 12.49pc for the one-year tenor at Wednesday’s T-bill auction. The hike in returns on risk-free government papers reflected a possible rise in the SBP policy rate at the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct 26. Mr Mamsa said the stable rupee helps contain imported inflation. Higher domestic fuel prices allow demand and imports to adjust. “The IMF, meanwhile, continues to emphasise a more market-based exchange rate. The authorities are reluctant to reopen the imported inflation Pandora’s Box,” he said, adding that a market-based exchange rate parity does not automatically mean a weaker rupee. “If remittances remain strong, reserves continue improving, the current account stays manageable, and the dollar demand remains contained, price discovery can still produce a stable currency,” he said. Analysis: Why lower inflation still feels expensive. A SLOWDOWN in inflation may offer some statistical relief to the government, but prices of everyday essentials remain substantially higher than they were two years ago. The apparent contradiction lies in the difference between what inflation measures and what consumers experience when they enter the market. Headline inflation measures how quickly the overall price basket is changing. It does not show how far the general price level has already risen. The official measure is based on prices collected from different markets and cities and combined into urban, rural and national indices. Therefore, a national average may not correspond to the retail price paid by an individual consumer in a particular market. Lower inflation does not mean prices have returned to previous levels. It simply means that they are rising more slowly on average. Consumers continue to bear the cumulative impact of price increases recorded in previous years. This helps explain why easing inflation has yet to translate into a comparable reduction in the cost of living. A comparison of Pakistan Bureau of Statistics prices between October 2024 and October 2026 illustrates the extent of that accumulated burden. Several essential food and energy items remained substantially more expensive than they were two years earlier, even though headline inflation later moderated. Among the sharpest increases were those in onions, electricity, diesel and petrol. Slower inflation masks cumulative rise in essential prices over past two years These individual price movements do not, of course, represent overall inflation, which is calculated from a weighted basket of goods and services. But they help explain the disconnect between official inflation readings and what consumers encounter in retail markets. Wheat flour provides one of the clearest examples. The national average price of a 20kg flour bag increased from Rs1,835 in October 2024 to Rs2,697 in October 2026 — an increase of 47 per cent. Beef with bone became 26.7pc more expensive, while the price of a 2.5kg tin of vegetable ghee rose by 18.5pc. Retail prices in individual markets can be even higher than these national averages. The increases were steeper in transport fuels. Petrol rose from Rs248.18 per litre in October 2024 to Rs389.51 in October 2026, an increase of 56.9pc. High-speed diesel increased from Rs252.43 to Rs402.53 per litre over the same period, a rise of 59.5pc. This is where the distinction between inflation and the price level becomes especially important. Inflation captures the pace at which prices are changing across a weighted basket. By contrast, consumers confront the actual price level when buying flour, meat, fuel and other necessities. Several factors are contributing to the current price pressures, but former economic adviser to the government Dr Ashfaq Hasan Khan attributes them largely to higher global energy prices and domestic food prices, particularly wheat. He said higher energy prices were a global phenomenon, but governments elsewhere had sought to cushion consumers by reducing the incidence of taxation. In Pakistan, he argued, the impact of higher international energy prices had been compounded by the petroleum levy. “The petroleum levy is the root cause of rising inflation in Pakistan, besides higher global energy and food prices,” Dr Khan said, referring to a levy of Rs85 per litre. He described the current pressures as predominantly from the supply side rather than the result of excessive consumer demand. That distinction matters for the choice of policy response, he argued. “IMF is pressurising Pakistan to devalue its exchange rate and also increase SBP policy rate,” he said. Under a conventional IMF stabilisation programme, tighter monetary policy is used to curb demand, helping contain inflation and ease balance-of-payments pressures. But if inflation is being driven mainly by energy costs, petroleum levies and food prices, higher interest rates do not directly address the underlying sources of the increase, Dr Khan argued. “Raising interest rates is not the right solution to supply-side inflation,” he said, referring to the IMF demand for an increase in interest rates. As per reports, Riyadh is planning an offensive to help the Yemeni government — which it backs — retake the strategically important Red Sea coast area from the pro-Iran Houthis, who captured it during a lightning offensive last month. Hostilities are continuing; there were reports on Saturday of both Riyadh and Sana’a being attacked . Meanwhile, members of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement are due to hold an emergency meeting to discuss the Yemen situation. Regarding Iran, the US has reportedly ordered thousands more troops, as well as an aircraft carrier group, to the Gulf. This mirrors the build-up of American forces around Iran before the US-Israeli assault targeted the Islamic Republic in late February. Top US officials have reportedly met at Camp David to discuss the Yemen and Iran files. Diplomacy, it seems, is giving way to more war in the Gulf and the wider Middle East. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is dire, with hundreds of thousands of people uprooted, while the UN says millions of Yemenis, including more than 2m infants, face acute hunger. If the Yemen war sucks in more regional states, it will complicate matters further. The best option, therefore, is for Muslim and Arab states to help restore the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire. The Houthi Ansarallah group must pledge to stop its attacks on Saudi Arabia, while ensuring free passage through Bab al-Mandeb. The Saudis, on their part, should consider lifting the blockade of Houthi territory, while encouraging all Yemeni factions to peacefully resolve the internal conflict. The Yemen war has been raging for over a decade, and previous external interventions have failed to end it; in fact, continued violence has exacerbated the humanitarian situation. With regard to Iran, it appears that President Donald Trump’s administration has halted kinetic action only till the November US midterms, and plans to restart hostilities after elections are out of the way. This would be a grave error. US-Israeli aggression has caused great loss of life in Iran as well as damage to infrastructure, while the global economy has been shell-shocked due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The world — particularly the states of the region — cannot afford more disruption and war. Mr Trump has turned down the recent Iranian proposal to open Hormuz. He should reconsider his strategy and restart dialogue with Tehran, while the Iranians should promise to reopen the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iran and eases sanctions. The US leader has hailed the exit of American troops from Iraq. He should work on a similar plan to bring his forces home from elsewhere in the Gulf and end the Iran war. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

Pakistan’s Russian dilemma. IT is difficult to imagine a single small gesture reducing decades-old hostility between two archrivals. Yet, such a moment was witnessed recently when Alok Dimri, India’s national coordinator for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, visited Islamabad for a meeting. Talking to the state media, he said he was happy to be in Pakistan. It was a simple statement, but perhaps one that may ease some of the cross-border bitterness. Mr Dimri said this while visiting the National Council of Arts in Islamabad. The heritage, art, and culture that Pakistan and India share have repeatedly fallen victim to toxic narratives designed to provoke hate. Yet the cultural link carries a powerful sense of mutual belonging. It may be premature to read too much into the Indian delegate’s visit or to view his words as evidence of a thaw after last May’s stand-off . Still, the episode offers some hope: if leaders on both sides choose to move forward, the dialogue could quickly regain momentum. However, optimism should be tempered — as should any expectation that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will arrive in Islamabad to attend the SCO summit. If he did, it would be a miracle, and the biggest surprise in decades — even bigger than Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to Islamabad in 1988 to attend the Saarc summit or Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s arrival in Lahore in 1999. Both occasions had generated enormous hope for peace between the two neighbours. What actually followed is a familiar story. Another miracle would be if Russian President Vladimir Putin attended the Islamabad SCO summit next year. Pakistan is more curious about this visit and hopes it may trigger a major shift in its geopolitics and ambitions in Central Asia, while influencing the regional discourse in ways that would irritate India. Pakistan would be keen to enhance its defence cooperation with Russia, but particularly interested in making some progress on the much-discussed railway from Moscow to Islamabad and establishing a freight corridor using existing 7,000-kilometre-long railway networks, with Pakistan linked to Russia through Central Asia and/or Iran. Over the decades, Pakistan, the Central Asian states, and Iran have conceived many transnational projects, and each time with great enthusiasm, yet none has materialised. Afghanistan is always made to bear the burden of the blame because of its complex relationship with Pakistan. Russia is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. Is it not interesting that the conventional wars fought by India and Pakistan collectively may not have lasted for more than a few weeks, and that Pakistan fought its longest war against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan? Pakistan and the Afghan mujahideen, together with the US, defeated the Russians, which was followed by the dismantling of the Soviet state. The Pakistani leadership still takes pride in that success. Of course, times have changed, and Pakistan is looking to cultivate new economic and defence opportunities. Russia, however, is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. This is not because of their bitter past, from which both sides have moved on, but because of divergent regional interests, particularly over Afghanistan, and Russia’s deep and long-standing engagement with India. Russian-Indian defence and economic cooperation is not necessarily an obstacle to developing ties with Pakistan. But it does mean that Islamabad cannot be regarded as a preferred partner in that context. The disparity in economic relations is significant: Pakistan’s bilateral trade with Russia is less than half a billion dollars, compared with around $69bn in India-Russia trade. The gap is even more pronounced in defence cooperation. India maintains a high level of military engagement with Russia through multiple military-technical cooperation frameworks, including joint research and development, co-development, co-production, and after-sales support. By contrast, Russia’s defence engagement with Pakistan remains selective and falls well short of a strategic military partnership. At the same time, India’s diversification of its defence partnerships has not significantly weakened its relationship with Russia. Moscow may have reservations about some aspects of New Delhi’s growing defence ties with other countries, but there are no clear signs of a fundamental deterioration in bilateral relations. Russia’s interest in Pakistan is, therefore, largely geopolitical — maintaining engagement with Islamabad allows Moscow to show that its international network of partnerships is broad, while also keeping channels open with Pakistan’s political and security leaders, including those who have close ties with US President Donald Trump. Public diplomacy is a domain through which Russia keeps its support club intact and seeks to enhance it, engaging Pakistani media, academics, opinion-makers, and policymakers through exchange programmes. The SCO is another platform Russia uses more extensively than other partners for public diplomacy. Russia and Pakistan share counterterrorism concerns, but their approaches to Afghanistan differ sharply. Russia has recognised the Taliban regime, but Pakistan is fighting a tough war against terrorism and sees Afghanistan as a source of the war. In geo-economic terms, they have different priorities. Russia wants Afgha­n­istan in the camp of its Central Asian allies. At the same time, Pakistan is a major partner of the US in areas where the interests of the two countries converge in Afghanistan. This irritates not only Russia but also China, which wants the US to stay out of the region in its immediate neighbourhood. The US took two decades to leave Afghanistan, and China does not want to see it coming back. It is not surprising that Indian-Russian relations have had few hiccups over decades. At the same time, Pakistan chose the US as its strategic partner after independence. Still, their relationship has not been smooth. Pakistan’s strategic partnership with China has also been tested recently, triggered by CPEC-related disputes and internal security concerns regarding Chinese nationals in Pakistan. Perhaps Russia is a new love interest for a segment of Pakistan’s power elite, but the two have little to share. And the last optimistic note: what if India and Pakistan decide to live in peace? What would the geopolitical impact be? The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

The court that could not see. WITNESSES testified that a senior banker sketched private parts on the glass of his desk, asked a woman colleague to name them, and threatened to tear off her clothes if she wore a particular outfit again. Another officer made indecent remarks about her attire before colleagues. The ombudsperson found the charges proved; the Islamabad High Court agreed. On Sept 16, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) set that judgement aside without substantively engaging with this evidence or the high court’s careful appraisal of it. Its central reason was a definition. Harassment under the 2010 workplace harassment law, it declared, “is only restricted to conduct which is sexual in nature”. Even by that narrow test, the conduct proved was plainly sexual. Before the high court, the officers never contended it fell short of harassment. Why does the FCC confine harassment to sex? The Act’s title and preamble speak of ‘harassment’, not ‘sexual harassment’, and anchor it in the right to dignity. Nor does ‘sexual’ mean only the act of sex; it also means relating to the sexes, or to gender. The Supreme Court said so on review in Nadia Naz, through Justice Ayesha Malik; “sexually demeaning attitudes” means demeaning a person because of their sex. Yale’s Vicki Schultz has shown that much workplace harassment has nothing to do with desire; it belittles women and signals they do not belong. And the 2022 amendment , ignored altogether, covers gender discrimination “which may or may not be sexual in nature”. Courts elsewhere agree. The US supreme court held in Oncale that harassment need not be motivated by desire; Canada and India root it in equality and dignity. India’s law lists “sexually coloured remarks”, exactly what was proved, and the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the FCC relies on quoted that very provision. ILO Convention 190 treats gender-based harassment, including sexual harassment, as one wrong. This is where a constitutional court should begin. Article 14 declares the dignity of man inviolable, and the Act’s own preamble rests on it. A constitutional court’s first duty is to read statutes through fundamental rights and expand their frontiers, not shrink them. A woman made to name drawings of private parts before her colleagues has had her dignity violated by any measure. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. Our Supreme Court had already arrived there. In Uzma Naveed (2022) and Muhammad Din (2025), both of which I authored, it held that harassment is not confined to the act of sex and that dignity is absolute and non-negotiable. The FCC dismisses Muhammad Din in one sentence, “with due respect”, ignores Uzma Naveed, and leans instead on the 2021 Nadia Naz judgement the Supreme Court set aside on review. In Haji Adam, decided by the same author the same day, substantial passages reappear word for word; it even names the bank case’s witnesses as the Pemra complainant’s. That raises a serious question whether each record received independent judicial consideration. Precedent is not a courtesy; it is law. Judgements of the Supreme Court delivered before the 27th Amendment bound every court under Article 189. The amendment operates prospectively: it makes the FCC’s decisions binding from now on, but it does not erase nearly eight decades of constitutional jurisprudence. Having inherited the Supreme Court’s constitutional jurisdiction, the FCC inherited the law declared under it. If it doubts that law, the doctrine of precedent requires reasoned reconsideration by a larger bench, not a three-member bench’s single sentence. Even the FCC’s own test, set this March, forbids precedent being “ignored and disregarded in silence”. The deeper problem is the court itself. It was created by the 27th Amendment, rushed through a parliament whose own mandate remains clouded by the disputed elections of February 2024, and carved out of a functioning Supreme Court for reasons never convincingly explained. Britain, the US, India, Canada and Australia entrust constitutional questions to a single apex court, and for good reason: splitting the apex invites conflict and political engineering. South Africa moved the other way in 2013, making its constitutional court the apex court in all matters. Its first bench was chosen by the president on the prime minister’s advice, bypassing the Judicial Commission, with no published criteria or open assessment of merit. Such a court must earn confidence through its work. A judgement rendered without hearing the attorney general or appointing an amicus (even the high court had one), and thin on scholarship and constitutional understanding, does not earn it. Nor does the price: salaries above the Supreme Court’s until that court was raised to match, generous staff allowances, and three more years of tenure. Not a single woman sits on the FCC, a conspicuous absence in a harassment case. I cast no aspersion on any judge who accepted appointment; that is for each conscience. Yet the absence speaks. The women of our judiciary stand apart from this court and deserve the country’s admiration. Such judgements belong to the bar too, for it is very much part of this new judicial era. Bar associations are guarantor institutions; in 2007 they marched until judges were restored. When the architecture of the 26th and 27th Amendments was assembled, that resistance never came. Too many at the bar’s helm measure ambition by proximity to power rather than fidelity to democracy. That is a deficit of character, not of numbers. When the guardians fall silent, unconstitutionalism rises. Constitutional courts are judged not by the powers they claim but by the rights they protect. If this is the direction of travel, dark years lie ahead for rights. Faiz urged us to speak while our lips are still free. It now falls to the lawyers who remember 2007, the academy and those who refuse to be silenced to keep the lamps lit. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Professor of Practice at SAHSOL, Lums and currently a Visiting Fellow at Yale University, US.
