Ireland news conference before Israel game cut short amid tensions. BACKA TOPOLA: The Republic of Ireland’s press conference on Saturday on the eve of their second Nations League match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists. Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary in their first match on Tuesday following a turbulent build-up in which the Irish squad voted to fulfil the fixture despite unease amongst the team over the war in Gaza. During that match the Irish players wore armbands and pointedly lowered their heads while the Israeli national anthem played. There were no handshakes between the captains before kickoff. With the return leg taking place on Sunday in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) refused to host the match at home for security reasons, it was the Ireland manager’s pre-match press conference that gave rise to new tensions. One journalist questioned Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday during a Flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel, which Emirati judicial authorities and Israeli officials have described as a “terrorist act”. “What do you say about the people that you support? Their ideology is based on murder,” one journalist asked. “Just this week, one of them tried to kill 170 Israeli passengers, including 27 innocent children and thousands of others.” An Irish press officer replied: “We are not doing any questions like this today. We are doing football questions.” Another journalist then addressed the Ireland manager: “Your players call our players monkeys during the match…”, only to be immediately interrupted by an FAI official repeatedly insisting “that is completely untrue,” while the microphone was taken away from the reporter in question. “Don’t touch me, don’t touch me,” the journalist exclaimed, as the Irish delegation brought the press conference to an abrupt end. ‘A lot of emotions’ Israeli authorities have condemned the actions taken by the Irish team, with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accusing Dublin of being on “the wrong side of history.” “Surviving this, coming out of it together as one would be a massive win for me. That is coming from my heart,” Hallgrimsson told journalists. “All the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism. “Just surviving as a group after this game, that would be a big win for me and for this group, for the association. “There’s been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well. “We want to do good, but it’s always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is. So we try to focus on the football side, and we’ve done a lot of things to help in that area. “One change that we’ve done in the last games is before we go onto the pitch, we do a little prayer and a huddle with the players and all the staff, just to cool our heads before we go onto the pitch. “Conor Coventry has taken that part, so he is now called Brother Coventry in the squad. But it’s really good when you go into a high-intensity and big-pressure game like we’ve been doing, to start the game with cool heads.” Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

Burglars steal antiques belonging to Nawab of Bahawalpur’s family in Islamabad. ISLAMABAD: Robbers and burglars stole cash and valuables worth over Rs34 million in eight incidents in the capital, police said. In the first incident, burglars stole priceless heirlooms and antiques belonging to the family of the Nawab of Bahawalpur, worth Rs20 million, from the house of Prince Bahawal Abbas Khan Abbasi, son of Nawab Salahuddin Abbasi, in F-8/3. Police registered a case under Sections 454 and 380 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). The incident came to light when the family found the storeroom broken into and the heirlooms and antiques missing. The stolen items included silver and gold articles, including a silver throne chair, silver ladder, silver bowls, silver statues, gold plates, Bahawalpur-crested gold plates and a large crested silver frame bearing the Bahawalpur State crest. Antique arms and heritage weapons, including old musket guns and swords of the Bahawalpur State, were also found missing, along with other valuable articles. The complainant told police that stock-taking and inventory were in progress and that a supplementary list of other missing items would be submitted once the inventory was completed. In the second incident, a gang of robbers looted cash and gold worth Rs3 million from the house of Ali Akbar Naqvi in Naval Anchorage. Four armed men raided the house and held Naqvi’s parents hostage at gunpoint. They then ransacked the house and took eight tolas of gold, a dozen silver rings, two watches, Rs100,000 in cash and other items before escaping. In another incident, a man allegedly looted cash and gold worth Rs2.3 million from a house in Margalla Town. The suspect entered Ali Ashgar’s house by impersonating someone and allegedly threatened the family with dire consequences. Meanwhile, a gang of robbers allegedly snatched a motorcycle from a man in Abbasiabad. Two armed men intercepted Safi Ullah and held him at gunpoint before taking his motorcycle, mobile phone and Rs300,000 in cash. Likewise, burglars stole cash and gold worth over Rs4.4 million from the house of Mohammad Bilal in D-12. The incident took place when the residents had gone to Murree. On their return, they found the house ransacked. Similarly, burglars stole cash and gold from the house of Wasim Ikhlas in Alipur. Moreover, burglars stole cash and valuables worth over Rs4.5 million from the house of Nabil Shahzad in Sri Saral. In another incident, thieves allegedly stole 28 iPhones worth Rs8 million from the house of Ammar Farooq in DHA Phase II. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

4 injured Pakistanis rescued from vessel hijacked in Somalia head to Karachi with remains of 3 colleagues. The four Pakistanis who were injured during a security operation to recover a hijacked oil tanker off the coast of Somalia, along with the remains of three others who lost their lives in the episode, have departed Addis Ababa and are expected to reach Karachi Sunday evening. “Pakistan’s ambassadors to Djibouti and Ethiopia saw off the four injured Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25 , Usman Ghani, Aqeel Khan, Ameen bin Shams and Yasir Khan, along with the mortal remains of Rafi Ullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmad Ansari, from Addis Ababa. “They are arriving in Karachi today aboard Ethiopian Airlines flight ET 694,” a post on the Foreign Office’s (FO) said. The seven were among 10 Pakistanis aboard MT Honour 25, which was hijacked by Somali pirates in April. Apart from Pakistanis, the vessel’s crew also included seven Indonesians, an Indian and a Sri Lankan. For around five months, there had been no progress either in negotiations or in the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for the recovery of the hostages, despite concerns abounding about their declining health. Since the hijacking, the crew made several emotional videos and audio appeals , reporting that they ran out of clean water, food and medicine. For its part, FO maintained that it remained “actively engaged” to secure the release of the sailors. On Sept 29, Somali maritime police recovered the Palau-flagged oil tanker amid reports of casualties among the crew. During the operation, it said, 21 suspected pirates were apprehended, while operations to locate the remaining members continue. “Before the operation [had] begun, the pirates on board the ship killed five of the crew. Among those killed were three from Pakistan, one from Myanmar and one from India,” it said. Advocate Quratulain of the Ansar Burney Trust, however, gave a separate account of the events, saying the pirates had brought the hostages onto the deck when they realised Puntland forces were approaching. “They tied their hands and warned to kill them if the police force came anywhere near them without paying them the ransom,” she said, adding that the ransom demand had by then been reduced from an initial $3 million to $1m. She said the pirates opened fire on the hostages as the security forces proceeded with the operation, killing three Pakistanis, one Indian and one Myanmar national. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has announced a relief package worth Rs12.5 million for the deceased sailors’ families.

Yemen forces say struck Houthi targets in several areas. Yemen’s government forces said Sunday they had struck Houthi targets around the country, deepening the conflict ravaging one of the world’s poorest nations and the wider region. The armed forces launched strikes against the Houthis in the capital Sanaa, the northwestern governorate of Saada — one of the group’s strongholds — and Taiz in the southwest, military spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said. Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July after years of calm, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa. The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east — a region that is larger but much less populated. The strikes came hours after the Houthis claimed an attack on an oil facility near the Saudi capital, where an AFP journalist saw flames and smoke, and accused the Gulf kingdom of striking Sanaa dozens of times. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive last month. Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that “Saudi enemy aircraft” hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting “Saudi aggression” against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties. Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city. In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said. While the Saudi authorities are yet to comment, late on Saturday, the Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, adding that they sparked fires at the targeted sites. The AFP journalist reported seeing firefighters scrambling to extinguish a blaze at Aramco’s Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah channel also reported missile strikes earlier on Saturday on the telecommunications network in Saada. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July. Hunger warning Hostilities between the Houthis and Yemen’s government had reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade. Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait. They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has worsened a humanitarian crisis sweeping Yemen, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Battle for Taiz Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday. The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died. The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis. While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to take control of Taiz city, Yemen’s third-largest after Sanaa and Aden. The Houthis also said on Friday that Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours. Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border. Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.

Security forces kill 8 terrorists in Dera Ismail Khan IBO: state media. Security forces killed eight terrorists during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Dera Ismail Khan, security sources said on Sunday, according to state-run Radio Pakistan . The terrorists were identified as those belonging to Fitna-al-Khawarij — a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan — the Radio Pakistan report said. Security sources said that three key terrorist commanders were among those killed and foreign currency and a large quantity of arms and ammunition was found in the possession of the slain terrorists. The IBO was a part of the Azm-i-Istehkam operation, the report added. Operation Azm-i-Istehkam was launched in June 2024, symbolising the national resolve to eradicate extremism and terrorism from the country. President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif commended security forces for timely and effective action in DI Khan. PM Shehbaz said in a statement that the Pakistani nation stood shoulder to shoulder with the security forces in the war against terrorism, Radio Pakistan reported. In a separate statement, President Asif Ali Zardari said the nefarious designs of “terrorists operating under foreign patronage and with the support of local facilitators will never be allowed to succeed”. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). In response to these incidents, security forces have been conducting operations in various parts of the province. On Saturday, state media reported that security forces had killed five Fitna al Khawarij terrorists during an IBO in KP’s South Waziristan district. On Friday, seven terrorists were killed in the Eidak area of KP’s North Waziristan district during an IBO. On Wednesday, security forces killed three terrorists in an IBO in KP’s Mir Ali. A day before that, in an IBO in KP’s Bara area, security forces killed five terrorists. On Monday, four terrorists were killed during an IBO in DI Khan. On Sept 17, security forces killed 10 terrorists in separate operations in KP between Sept 15 and 17. Earlier in the month, over 20 terrorists were killed during multiple engagements in KP between Sept 3 and 5. On Sept 18, a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation . On September 26 in DI Khan, 14 people, including two rescue officials, were martyred and 35 sustained injuries after a suicide bomber rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into a police checkpost and then targeted an ambulance shifting bodies to hospital.

Like a 'vertical roller coaster': Simulating flydubai flight FZ1073's sudden plunge. Flydubai’s flight FZ1073, which plunged 16,000 feet in about 30 seconds before being levelled out and landing safely, would have felt like a “vertical roller coaster”, according to an aviation instructor who recreated the descent in a flight simulator for Reuters . The steep fall, after an attack on the captain by the co-pilot during a flight on Wednesday, would have put huge strain on the Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft — as well as the passengers and crew, said Alberto Paduanelli, owner of ALPA Simulation in Sherfield on Loddon, southern England. The co-pilot of the flydubai jet, which was bound for Israel from Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, calling the incident a “ terrorist attack ”. The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, two sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters . UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity. Reuters could not independently reach al-Hammami for comment. Flydubai says the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation and it cannot comment further. Oman has yet to comment on the incident. “A plunge of 16,000 feet (4,877 metres) over 30 seconds will feel like you are over on a very, very vertical roller coaster,” Paduanelli said, sitting at the controls of the simulator cockpit. “The difference is that on the roller coaster, you know what’s happening,” he said, adding that with a sudden drop “you feel the negative g-force on your body”. For passengers who are not strapped in, “Your body will literally lift from the seat”, he said. Using a simulator to recreate the incident, Paduanelli said the aircraft’s autopilot disconnected before the plunge began, causing the jet to accelerate rapidly. United States President Donald Trump has praised the Boeing jet for withstanding the severe forces put on it during the incident. The plane was levelled out after passengers overpowered the co-pilot, before a reserve crew of pilots onboard landed the plane. “It was an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design,” Trump posted on Truth Social, adding that the 737 MAX “was able to withstand G Forces and Strain far beyond what it was designed and expected to do”. Boeing did not respond to a request for comment. Aircraft are designed and tested to withstand substantial aerodynamic loads, but Paduanelli said a prolonged high-speed dive can place extreme strain on an airframe. “This was nothing but a miracle that nothing was hurt apart from the captain, unfortunately, and that two pilots were onboard,” Paduanelli said. Details about al-Hammami’s past have trickled out. Royal Air Maroc told Reuters he did a three-month training with the airline in 2025 but his application to work there afterwards was rejected. Buckinghamshire New University in Britain said he did a distance-learning course in aviation management with the institution, but no pilot training. An Australian Federal Police spokesperson said on Sunday that authorities there were investigating al-Hammami’s “links to Australia”. A source briefed on the investigation said the co-pilot studied at a university in Melbourne.

Naqvi says talks with opposition have collapsed, accuses KP CM of 'sabotaging' negotiations. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Sunday that the talks between the federal government and the opposition had collapsed as the PTI had initiated its long march, accusing Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi of “sabotaging” the negotiations. Naqvi was addressing a press conference in Islamabad hours after an hours-long second round of talks between the two sides ended without yielding any results. “Their team was reasonable. I am repeating that I will not blame anyone else for all of this collapsing. There is only one person responsible for the entire collapse, and that is the KP chief minister,” the interior minister declared. He further said that Afridi was to be responsible “if there is any loss of life”. He said those supporting the PTI leader should “realise that they will be committing contempt of court, and we will take legal action against them to every possible extent”. He warned that no one would be allowed to violate the Islamabad High Court’s order regarding protest. The IHC order , issued on Sept 14, ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”. Notably, Naqvi stressed that there “had been no request from our side for the long march to be postponed”. “When we had the first meeting, we told them that the long march was not an issue for us. However, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto had already given an indication and had also given a date. A day earlier, he had said that the PPP wanted the long march to be postponed and for the temperature to be brought down,” he added. Naqvi explained that the PTI was given the option to hold a protest but would not allow an attempt to “create a disturbance”. “We gave them this option. Now, if they violate the orders, whether they are workers or politicians, whether they are protesting within KP or outside KP, we will pursue them one by one. This time, we want to ensure that this repeated episode of creating a disturbance in Islamabad comes to an end,” he asserted. According to the interior minister, there were two agreements to be reached — one was a “main agreement” that would cover whatever was being decided with the opposition parties, and the other was regarding counterterrorism. “If we had known that no one in this committee was authorised to give a commitment on behalf of the KP government, or that the KP government would veto all these things, we would not have held the negotiations in this form in the first place,” he remarked. The minister said the two sides had agreed “100 per cent on political things” so that the KP government could come on board with the Centre on the counterterrorism issues. “It is not appropriate that there is a war going on in one province and the ministers there are giving statements against the army, are not coming to funerals, and at the local level, somewhere or the other, terrorists are also being given support,” he added. “If there is a military operation, would you tell the army which gun to use or which drone to use? This happens nowhere in the world,” he said. Naqvi detailed Saturday’s developments: “I requested CM Afridi to onboard the KP government because, definitely, the problems we are facing are coming from the KP government. He said, ‘Okay, I am going now,’ so we postponed the meeting until tomorrow. All members agreed to the postponement. “They (opposition team) held negotiations with CM Afridi for four hours. The KP CM gave them his feedback and gave them the mandate that whatever they finalise with him, they should proceed with it.” The interior minister accused Afridi of changing the draft of the agreement despite what had been agreed to earlier. “When I forwarded the draft to the KP chief minister, around 9pm he became active. Once the draft is finalised, he asks for changes once and then asks again, and by 12am or 12:30am at night, he brings an entirely new draft. And in that, he changed the things that we had locked after discussing them,” Naqvi asserted. In an apparent jibe at the KP CM, Naqvi noted that placing “immature and inexperienced people in positions of authority had consequences for the country”. “You have seen in the past how chief ministers came to this province and the country continued to suffer the consequences. Similarly, if an immature boy sits in a position of authority, has no experience and has not seen politics, then definitely he will call himself a representative of the people, but he will make decisions in the same way as my team and I witnessed yesterday.” Commending the government’s delegation, the minister said: “They worked non-stop for 12 hours and, even before that, made sincere efforts to resolve the issue. I will give them credit for the fact that at no point did they say no. They remained focused on resolving the matter. From the smallest issue to the major ones, all the members made a sincere effort to resolve them in a good manner.” Conditions and demands Earlier in the day, Naqvi also claimed on X that the KP government had agreed to sign a written agreement and submit an implementation plan within 72 hours, mainly covering counterterrorism initiatives, during the talks held over the weekend, but then backtracked. According to Naqvi, the PTI had agreed to: Reconsider the Police Act 2026 in light of the security situation and the need to protect security matters from political interference Prevent terrorists from operating freely or finding safe havens in the province Unequivocal condemnation of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan and all other terrorist groups Support the national policy on Afghan refugees, including repatriation and dismantling Afghan camps in KP No contact with the interim Afghan government Substantial funding for counterterrorism operations and the police Full provincial ownership of counterterrorism measures and stronger cooperation with the armed forces Decisions on counterterrorism in the former Fata and merged districts Implementation of the National Action Plan “Last night, during the final phase of negotiations, the KP government backed out of these commitments. Security must not be politicised while the province is at war,” he said. The meeting between the opposition and federal government at Parliament House began after 4pm on Saturday, with discussions focusing on the PTI’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad. The talks extended into the early hours of Sunday without yielding any results. However, shortly before 3am on Sunday, Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, who was part of the opposition delegation, told the media that the talks had not resulted in a breakthrough. He went on to say that the deadlock was over jailed PTI founder Imran Khan’s meeting with his personal physicians, and how to address terrorism in KP. But Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, who was part of the government’s delegation, said the talks failed primarily because the “KP government could not assure whether they would cooperate in the fight against terrorism in the future”. He alleged that the PTI’s provincial government in KP did not want to implement the NAP and that the PTI delegation that participated in the talks had also left the venue “disappointed because the KP government did not cooperate on terrorism”. Following these allegations, CM Afridi posted on X that he was sharing the text of the draft he sent to the opposition’s negotiating team, saying that “no even one demand in there was unconstitutional or illegal”. He then went on to list the demands, calling for: Arrangements for meetings between the prime minister and the leaders of the opposition in both houses of Parliament to discuss important political, national, constitutional, legal, and democratic issues, particularly those facing delays. “The two sides shall be bound to ensure effective and feasible progress within two months towards resolving the aforementioned matters through mutual consultation and negotiations.” The prime minister to form a joint political negotiating committee comprising representatives from the ruling coalition, the PPP and opposition parties. “This committee shall engage in continuous negotiations with the opposition on national and political matters, points of disagreement, and other important issues, and shall seek feasible solutions through mutual consensus. The committee shall ensure significant progress on negotiations and resolutions within one month of its formation and shall present its recommendations to the relevant leadership.” Ensuring all legal, human and medical rights for Imran and his spouse, Bushra Bibi, in accordance with the jail manual, Constitution and prevailing laws. “Where legally applicable, necessary medical facilities and treatment shall be provided to them, taking into account the opinion, instructions and advice of their personal or nominated physicians.” Allowing Imran and Bushra Bibi to meet their family members, lawyers and other associates, in accordance with the jail manual and relevant laws. “Such meetings shall be conducted in accordance with the law and jail rules and regulations. However, the facility of meetings will not be used by any party for political or other purposes prohibited by law.” The process of taking up appeals filed by prisoners against their sentences to be initiated or completed within 10 days, where legally possible, in accordance with the Constitution and law. “All cases shall be decided by the relevant courts and legal forums in accordance with the Constitution, law, transparent judicial procedures and principles of justice, without undue delay. And women who are political prisoners, including Yasmin Rashid and Bushra Bibi, should be released expeditiously on humanitarian grounds.” Effective, continuous and meaningful consultation between the federal and provincial governments to eradicate terrorism, protect the lives and property of the people and establish lasting peace in KP. “Existing policies and measures should be reviewed and amended as needed.” Authorised representatives of the federal and provincial governments shall convene regular meetings within 72 hours and, through mutual consultation, formulate a clear, comprehensive and feasible strategy for peace and security. The implementation of this strategy, within the scope of the Constitution and law, shall be the joint responsibility of the federal and provincial governments.” The KP CM said that PTI would announce the cancellation of the long march upon receiving a written assurance from the federal government for the effective implementation of the aforementioned assurances and agreed actions. “However, if the federal government violates the agreed assurances, the negotiation process, or constitutional and legal requirements, or causes undue disruption to the negotiation process, PTI shall reserve the right to peaceful, democratic and lawful protest in accordance with the Constitution and law”, he added.

KP CM Afridi reaches Lakki Marwat to lead PTI march on Islamabad. PESHAWAR/LAKKI MARWAT/DI KHAN: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi reached Lakki Marwat by helicopter on Sunday to lead the PTI’s long march, which is being carried out to demand the release of jailed party founder and ex-prime minister Imran Khan, from Gandi Chowk on the Peshawar-Karachi Indus Highway. A special helipad was prepared near Maidadkhel for the arrival of the chief minister, and a video shared on social media platforms showed a crowd of PTI workers gathered around it as KP’s chief executive touched down. A video shared by the PTI on its X account showed Afridi’s convoy setting off, surrounded by a large crowd of party workers and supporters. However, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar criticised Afridi in a post on X for using a “state helicopter for a political march”. Calling the use of the helicopter a “violation of the Islamabad High Court’s orders”, he wrote, “Terrorism is spreading in the province and Nero is playing his flute.” Earlier, PTI workers and supporters, led by former Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Ali Amin Gandapur, set out from Dera Ismail Khan for the party’s long march. Before departing from DI Khan, Gandapur stressed that the protest should remain peaceful and urged the participants to maintain discipline and refrain from violence, vandalism and confrontation with law enforcement personnel. He said the party would follow a policy of “live and let live” during the protest and directed workers not to take the law into their hands. “Those who block roads or engage in confrontation are not our workers,” Gandapur said, asking the participants to remain peaceful throughout the march. He further urged the participants to avoid any activity that could lead to clashes or damage to public or private property. Describing the march as a continuation of the party’s political struggle, Gandapur said it represented a reaffirmation of the party’s commitment to PTI founder Imran. “We have made sacrifices for Imran Khan before and will not hesitate to make further sacrifices,” he said, adding that the party would continue its “peaceful political struggle” for Imran’s release. The convoy, according to Gandapur, would travel through Yarik and Pezu before reaching Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat. Meanwhile, on the Peshawar-Karachi Highway near Serai Naurang in Gandi Chowk, PTI workers had started gathering on Sunday afternoon to participate in the long march. Strict security measures were in place, with a large police contingent deployed at the site along with armoured personnel carriers and bomb disposal squads. Special Assistant to the KP chief minister for Home and Tribal Affairs Tariq Saad told journalists at his residence that, in accordance with the PTI leadership’s decision, the “peaceful long” march would commence from Gandi Chowk today, with convoys from the southern districts joining it. He said PTI workers from Bannu, DI Khan, Tank, North Waziristan and South Waziristan would gather at Gandi Chowk to participate in the march. “If workers from some southern districts, especially Tank and Waziristan, could not attend the long march today due to law and order-related curfew and other restrictions, they would join the movement on the way to Peshawar the next day,” he said. The PTI’s march, being carried out to demand the release of its jailed founder and ex-prime minister Imran Khan, is the latest bone of contention between the two sides. In August, the PTI announced the long march to Islamabad on Sept 27 against what it called the “illegal imprisonment” of its party founder. However, a couple of days before its scheduled long march, the party postponed the march until Oct 4 (today). Meanwhile, federal ministers have warned that the Centre would have no option but to impose governor’s rule or an emergency in KP, citing the province’s security situation and the protest call, while PTI has warned of dire consequences if such a step was taken. After weekend talks, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah has further warned that the protesters will not be allowed to enter Islamabad. Plan for the march According to the plan for the march shared by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister on X, PTI supporters from the districts of Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South Waziristan, North Waziristan and Bannu will join the long march from Lakki Marwat’s Gandi Chowk on Oct 4. The caravan will halt for the night near Karak, from where people will depart at 12:30pm the next day and stay overnight near Kohat. Then, at 12pm on Oct 6, protesters from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram, and Orakzai will join the convoy, which will move towards Peshawar and spend the night near Mattani. The caravan will depart from Budh Bair in Peshawar on Oct 7 afternoon. “The remaining constituencies of Peshawar will join us at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza. And we will spend the night near Charsadda Interchange,” the KP CM said. They would then depart the Charsadda Interchange at 12:30pm on Oct 8 after people from Charsadda and Mohmand join them. Refraining from detailing the final leg of the trip to the federal capital, Afridi said the people “of entire KP” would gather at Khairabad on Oct 8 and spend the night there. “God willing, the plan for the next phase will be announced there.” Ahead of the march, movement on several roads on KP has been banned under Section 144. Section 144 imposed in several KP districts Section 144 has been imposed in several districts of KP through notifications issued by the respective deputy commissioners, with restrictions on the movement of people and vehicles along specified routes, citing security and public safety concerns. In DI Khan, restrictions have been imposed under Section 144 from October 4 to October 6, from 6am to 6pm, banning the movement of individuals and all types of traffic on specified roads and routes, citing the prevailing law-and-order situation and public safety concerns. In South Waziristan Upper, Section 144 has been imposed from October 3 to October 5, banning the movement of cargo vehicles, rickshaws and dumpers over a possible VBSB/VBIED threat in adjoining areas. In South Waziristan Lower, restrictions have been imposed under Section 144 from October 1 to October 10, banning the movement of loader rickshaws, single- and double-cabin cargo vehicles, Shahzore vehicles, Mazdas, Suzuki loaders and dumpers in Wana and Azam Warsak. The notification cited security and public safety concerns. In District Tank, restrictions have been imposed under Section 144 from 9pm on Oct 3 until noon on Oct 5, restricting the movement of individuals and all types of traffic along specified routes. The notification cited the prevailing law-and-order situation, public safety concerns and the need to ensure the safe movement of law-enforcement personnel. In Hangu, restrictions have been imposed under Section 144 from October 3 to October 6, banning the movement of individuals and all types of traffic on six routes, including the Hangu-Kohat, Hangu-Thall, Hangu Bypass and Hangu-Sumari roads. The restrictions do not apply to law-enforcement agencies and emergency services, while exemptions may be granted by the district police officer or security forces.

Railways to outsource 13 passenger trains by December. LAHORE: The Pakistan Railways (PR) has decided to outsource 13 express passenger trains and directed its officers to complete the process by December this year. The department has also accelerated efforts to make all faulty (dummy) wagons fit for operation while taking action against the vendors who failed to supply parts on time. “It is the vision of the prime minister as well as mine to make all-out efforts to maintain the railway infrastructure for safe train operation. This is why I have assigned the officers concerned the task to accomplish the target of making all dummy coaches and wagons fit for operation,” Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi explained while talking to Dawn . “I have also asked the officers to replace the faulty brake cylinders, blocks and shoes with new ones,” he added. According to the minister, the outsourcing of trains and luggage vans is also underway and 13 express passenger trains would be outsourced till Dec 31. For this, the process, including the advertisement and award of the contract, would be completed soon. “At present, the commercial operation of six trains is being carried out by the private parties,” Mr Abbasi said, adding that the trains to be outsourced by December included Sandal, Allama Iqbal Express, Faiz Ahmad Faiz, Fareed Express, Sukkur Express, Babu Passenger, Bulleh Shah Passenger, Mohenjodaro Express, Lasani Express, Sialkot Express, Karachi Express, Bahauddin Zakariya Express and Tezgam. To a question, he said the railway bridge affected by the recent floods on Lahore-Faisalabad track would be rehabilitated within the next two months, helping railways to restore the rail traffic. For the first time, according to him, the freight revenue exceeded the passenger revenue in the railways. “I think, the railways would be able to earn revenue of Rs120bn from the passenger and freight train operations alone by the end of the ongoing fiscal year on June 30,” he hoped. Meanwhile, the minister presided over a meeting at the railway headquarters and directed the authorities to blacklist private vendors responsible for delays in the supply of equipment and materials. During the meeting, matters pertaining to railway operations, revenue generation, maintenance, security and outsourcing came under discussion. Mr Abbasi directed the authorities to install modern CCTV cameras and deploy private security personnel at all railway workshops and yards to prevent theft. He said collective efforts were required to achieve the revenue targets set for the current financial year, adding that locomotives undergoing repairs should be restored to service according to the prescribed schedule. The minister ordered legal action against negligent officials. The meeting was also told by the officers concerned that advance planning was essential for ensuring transparency and improving the railway system. He further directed that the ongoing track renewal work in Sukkur division should be completed by Dec 31 as it would save operational time by around one-and-a-half hours. He also ordered that the flood-damaged Mian Kallar Bridge be completed within 60 days and repair of employees’ residential quarters in Lahore within two months. Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

The UN’s High Level Week, Secretary-General Selection and “Middle Power” Problem hschaub Fri, 09/18/2026 - 17:29 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Global 18 September 2026 1 minute The UN’s High Level Week, Secretary-General Selection and “Middle Power” Problem This week on Hold Your Fire!, Richard Atwood is joined by Crisis Group experts Richard Gowan and Daniel Forti to discuss next week’s UN General Assembly high-level week and whether a new Secretary-General can revive the organisation’s peacemaking as global turmoil spreads. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy In this episode of Hold Your Fire! , Richard Atwood speaks with Richard Gowan, Crisis Group’s Director for Global Issues and Institutions, and Daniel Forti, Head of UN affairs, ahead of next week’s UN General Assembly high-level week. They explore the mood at the UN, its shifting relations with Washington and its shrinking role in peacemaking worldwide, particularly in the Middle East. They assess current Secretary-General António Guterres’s legacy, the contenders to succeed him and whether new leadership can reinvigorate the organisation’s peacemaking while defending the UN Charter’s principles and rebuilding relationships with powerful states. They also discuss how UN peacekeeping missions can adapt to fragile ceasefires and how much Western and non-Western mid-sized powers, which appear increasingly drawn to other forums, will invest in the UN’s future. Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms pfranz Fri, 09/18/2026 - 21:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Somali police officers walk along a road median while patrolling a busy street in Mogadishu, on November 10, 2025. TONY KARUMBA / AFP Commentary / Africa 18 September 2026 16 minutes Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms The multilateral missions that have helped the Somali government fight Al-Shabaab for nearly two decades may be coming to an end. Mogadishu and its partners should get started now developing a plan for what they will do next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia The multilateral missions that have protected Somalia’s government from the jihadist insurgent group Al-Shabaab since 2007 could be drawing to a close. In early July, the U.S. informed the African Union (AU) that it would not back an extension of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) – which provides crucial logistical assistance to the AU’s Support and Stabilisation Mission – beyond the end of its current mandate in December. The U.S. position has subsequently softened, with U.S. diplomats telling the AU in September that Washington would consider a twelve-month extension before calling a stop to further UN aid. This development buys time for a more orderly drawdown or some kind of transition. But the reality remains inescapable: the security blanket that Somalia has lived under for almost two decades is on borrowed time. The forthcoming UN General Assembly provides a prime opportunity for the Somali government, the AU and its security partners to kickstart essential discussions about how to keep Somalia safe. Given the AU mission’s reliance on the UN to provide water, food, fuel and transport, it will almost certainly be unable to continue in anything like its present form without UN help. The AU, its foreign partners and the Somali federal government are considering how to keep the mission going, but they do not have any particularly enticing options in mind. There is no clear alternative to the UN office, whose budget is nearly half a billion dollars, when it comes to setting up, running and paying for a multinational force. That said, predictions that the prospective end of UN and possibly AU security assistance will see the government collapse and Al-Shabaab emerge victorious are wide of the mark. While Al-Shabaab remains a major threat to the Somali government and controls swathes of southern and central Somalia, the group is largely confined to rural areas. The government’s grip extends to most urban centres, with security in the capital Mogadishu improving sharply in recent years. Support from the UN has helped maintain this precarious status quo. But an end to multilateral assistance need not culminate in the federal state’s downfall, even if a mismanaged transition could spell trouble. A combination of Somali and other international forces, including those already stationed in the country, should form part of a new international security structure. It is now up to Mogadishu and its international partners to begin planning this shift before it is too late. Approximate areas of operation for AUSSOM troop contributors. Some troop contributors maintain bilateral contingents in addition to their AUSSOM deployments. Source: Crisis Group research as of September 2026. CRISIS GROUP More Trouble for a Struggling Mission The AU mission and its UN logistics support office – the mainstay of foreign assistance for Somalia’s security – rely on troops from Africa and funds from farther afield. Ugandan troops were the first to be deployed upon the mission’s launch in 2007, followed soon thereafter by forces from Burundi and Djibouti. Kenya and Ethiopia joined in 2012 and 2014, respectively, after first launching their own bilateral interventions to safeguard their borders from Al-Shabaab incursions. The mission pushed the jihadist group out of many urban centres in south-central Somalia in the 2010s, including Mogadishu in 2011. More recently, however, the AU has struggled to find money for the mission, with long-time donors like the EU whittling down their contributions and pushing for the exit door. The mission has been running a large deficit for several years, even as it has taken measures to cut spending. Troop numbers have dwindled from 22,000 in the mid-2010s to around 12,000 today. Instead of launching offensive operations deep in the hinterlands controlled by Al-Shabaab, the mission has turned more toward protecting urban areas it already holds, while playing a supporting role in Somali army campaigns. The financial crunch has since extended to the UN’s logistical support, funded through UN assessed contributions – mandatory dues paid by all member states to underwrite the global body’s operations. Even before the Trump administration took office, U.S. officials were wary of the model that sees UN finances flow to a non-UN mission, regarding it as an undesirable precedent. In early 2025, the U.S. blocked a proposal for the AU mission to also receive funding through UN assessed contributions, arguing in part that the UN is already spending heavily on UNSOS. In September 2025, the U.S. shelved planned contributions to the UN peacekeeping budget, including for UNSOS. Hence, its refusal to support the office’s existence any further does not come as a complete surprise. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Despite this apparent contradiction, the U.S. government believes that the status quo is no longer tenable: the multilateral missions are not as effective as they once were, while the Somali government should bear the primary responsibility for leading the fight with Al-Shabaab. U.S. diplomats believe that Somali elites are skirting their duties, preoccupied with pursuing political vendettas rather than combating jihadists. It is difficult to know if President Donald Trump’s evident personal animus toward Somalia has also played a role. A number of U.S. officials agree that ending UNSOS, and by extension threatening the existence of the AU mission, is a risk. It was probably for this reason that the U.S. backtracked in September to grant the UN mission an additional twelve months to draw down. But this move only defers rather than eliminates the challenges ahead. The U.S. argues that Mogadishu can keep Al-Shabaab at bay by enhancing the deployment of Somali forces, and combining this measure with assistance from abroad, including troops from neighbouring countries and air support from the U.S. and Türkiye. The U.S. says it remains ready to contribute to fighting Al-Shabaab. It just no longer wants to do so through a multilateral vehicle that it regards as an unnecessary expense. Are There Alternatives to UNSOS? The drawdown and eventual closure of UNSOS would, in effect, mean that the AU mission could not continue as currently designed. The UN mission keeps AU troops supplied with food, water and fuel, sustaining nearly 50 bases across southern Somalia. It also provides transport for AU deployments. When funds permit, it supports Somali soldiers operating alongside the AU personnel. Privately, AU officials say the mission cannot continue without UN support: one termed the U.S. decision on the UNOSOS mandate “life-threatening”. Even with a twelve-month stay of execution, the UN support office’s coming year will be focused on winding down its extensive logistical responsibilities. Deciding what comes next has become imperative for the Somali authorities. A few options for logistical assistance for the AU mission have been mooted, but all face serious drawbacks. In July, the Somali government, the AU and troop-contributing states met in the Ugandan capital Kampala to discuss the mission’s future. They endorsed a plan for uninterrupted support for another eighteen to 24 months, a period that would be used to carry out offensives against Al-Shabaab and a more gradual drawdown. For Washington, however, an extension of UN support beyond what is now on the table is out of the question, a stance it communicated in September. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. But given the AU’s lack of experience in running such a complex operation, this option appears unworkable in the near term. The AU could subcontract logistics to a private company, but diplomats note that it would take up to two years to establish a mission with capabilities similar to those of UNSOS. Even if it were possible, the financial crunch would not vanish. With the AU mission unable even to cover troop stipends, there is no way at present that it could shoulder the costs of logistics. The deeper pockets of partners alarmed by the possibility of an imminent worsening of Somali security, such as the EU or Gulf Arab countries, might be prised open to an extent. But with so many other crises competing for resources, a donor boost remains a long shot. Alternatively, the AU could take whatever funding is available from the EU and others, channelling it toward covering troop stipends and the logistics of a smaller mission. This option would enable the AU to maintain its presence, but only by sacrificing its operational clout, perhaps by retrenching at a few key locations, most likely in and around Mogadishu and regional capitals. But countries contributing troops to the AU mission already argue they do not have enough personnel to protect themselves, let alone undertake forward operations. Reducing their numbers further could end up at a point where the mission is unable to defend itself or others from Al-Shabaab attack. With limited funding committed for 2026 and nothing beyond that, the AU might also find it difficult to win donors over to the idea of supporting a less effective version of the same mission. A further variant of this option is being floated in Addis Ababa, where the AU has its headquarters: reconfiguring the mission under a new regional mechanism, but still with an AU mandate. In this scenario, many of the African troops deployed in Somalia would stay, but under a setup not unlike the Multinational Joint Task Force in the Lake Chad basin, a regional initiative to combat Boko Haram. Parallels with the Lake Chad basin are imperfect, however: the various national militaries operating there largely do so inside their own frontiers, coordinating more on cross-border matters. The proposal also offers little by way of a solution to the logistics and funding dilemmas, simply passing the buck to troop-contributing states. One or another of these options might emerge to enable Somalia’s multilateral security support to stagger on past 2027. The U.S. decision to grant an extra twelve months buys time to evaluate all the options and allows for less haste in the overhaul. But one way or another, a transition, with all its uncertainties, appears imminent. Turning to Somali Forces The AU’s exit strategy is premised on Somali forces standing ready to take the mission’s place when it finally shuts down. There is no doubt that the Somali National Army has boosted its strength in recent years, generating upward of 10,000 new troops under training schemes supported by foreign partners like Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates and Eritrea. But it is still ill-prepared to fully and rapidly take the AU mission’s place. Certain areas handed over by the mission to Somali forces in recent years have later fallen into Al-Shabaab’s hands. Even when the Somali army has led operations against Al-Shabaab, such as in Lower Shabelle in 2025-2026, it has remained dependent on external support. Somali officials have argued for many years that they can take full responsibility for security, but that they need more time. Many in the current government and its predecessors have wanted Somali forces to step up, only to find themselves hamstrung by political rifts within the federal system that have weakened the national security apparatus. State-level forces are generally underdeveloped, while the divisions between federal officials and leaders in Puntland and Jubaland, who are at loggerheads over how power and resources are divided in Somalia’s federal system, hinder the emergence of a unified national army. During times of political crisis, such as the election-related turmoil at present, federal and state forces sometimes turn their guns on each other. These shortcomings have driven Mogadishu to establish a series of bilateral security agreements with Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia, ensuring that their troops will stay despite the AU mission’s withdrawal. Uganda reportedly has a force of around 2,000 troops stationed in and around Mogadishu, while Kenya and Ethiopia retain larger contingents closer to their own borders. Bilateral foreign forces in Somalia have remained stable even as the AU mission shrinks, a trend that will probably continue after its eventual departure. What Could a New Security Approach Look Like? The AU mission’s future is for now unclear. While replacing support from the UN, and possibly finding a substitute for the mission, would undoubtedly be a huge undertaking, the situation is not hopeless. With proper planning, political leadership and a measure of continued foreign backing, the Somali government should be able to shift from dependence on a multilateral force to a series of bilateral relationships that prevent a major security breakdown and sweeping military gains by Al-Shabaab. That said, there is little doubt that the impending loss of the UN support office’s annual spending on Somali security needs will cause headaches. Even if the AU manages somehow to retain a presence, the most likely shape of Somalia’s future security support will derive chiefly from the deeply rooted interests of Mogadishu’s foreign partners. Key members of the AU mission, particularly Kenya and Ethiopia, are primarily motivated by border security, particularly the desire to maintain a buffer against Al-Shabaab. Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni views his country’s longstanding deployment as a key part of his legacy. He likely holds out hope that Mogadishu will be able to find a donor to pay for Ugandan units stationed around the capital. From outside the region, Türkiye has become Somalia’s most important bilateral partner in recent years, training thousands of Somali troops as well as deploying advanced military assets like drones and F-16s. Ankara also remains keen to protect its wide-ranging strategic investments in the country. The U.S., for its part, asserts that it will, for now, maintain its bilateral counter-terrorism operations, particularly its drone program. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes, regardless of what happens to the AU mission, while buying more time for the Somali military to assume greater responsibility. The AU mission’s major troop contributors would ideally keep most of their contingents where they are, arranging their own logistics in the process, but changes are likely. The loss of UNSOS assistance will probably spur Kenya and Ethiopia into consolidating positions nearer their own borders, while Uganda will probably focus more on protecting Mogadishu and its environs. Smaller troop contributors like Burundi and Djibouti, on the other hand, may be less inclined to continue without additional support. In areas where foreign troops do withdraw, Somali forces should prepare to take over. Mogadishu claimed in early August that it has 14,000 troops available for military operations, who could instead be deployed as holding forces to take the place of departing AU personnel. Somali troops tend not to be as well trained or equipped as their AU counterparts, however, making a one-to-one switch from AU to Somali soldiers a hazardous proposition. Taking these steps might contain Al-Shabaab to its rural bastions and avoid the loss of major cities. Proper coordination with bilateral forces could help protect the most strategically important areas, including towns, infrastructure and supply routes. But a modest fallback from some of the positions that are now under the AU mission’s control seems inevitable. Uganda, for example, maintains more than a dozen bases in the Lower Shabelle region, which will be difficult to hold without UNSOS logistical support. Smaller towns surrounded by Al-Shabaab, such as Qoryoley, could be at risk of falling to the insurgents once the AU pulls out. Parts of Hirshabelle would also be vulnerable due to the concentration of Al-Shabaab forces in the area since 2025, adding pressure to towns along the main road in the state, such as Jalalaqsi. Even small losses could give momentum back to Al-Shabaab, while the capture of roads and economic centres would help sustain the group financially. It may be possible over the coming years to keep parts of the battlefield tilted in the Somali authorities’ favour through the calibrated deployment of foreign troops, especially when it comes to the defence of urban centres and transport arteries. Still, the systemic challenges to Somali security thrown up by a radical change in security arrangements cannot be wished away. If they are left unaddressed, the danger will rise of greater government losses and an Al-Shabaab surge outside its rural strongholds. First, shifting the security burden onto African states will not resolve the funding problem unless donors and Somali officials take bold steps. If the AU wants to remain involved, it will have to do more to raise its own funds. If not, the AU mission’s current backers – primarily the EU and UK, which in 2025 together contributed approximately $90 million – could find ways to transfer this support to cover logistics and stipends for troop-contributing states from the region and Somali forces. Gulf Arab states, which number among Somalia’s key backers, may even be more inclined to support bilateral forces, viewing multilateral support as a poor investment because it translates into minimal diplomatic influence. Even though its resources are strained, the Somali government could also reduce the burden on foreign donors: the government has managed to raise domestic revenue in recent years and has even funded a number of internal military operations and deployments. The more it can take on, the less it will need to lobby the same donors on behalf of other African troop contributors. Secondly, the Somali government, troop-contributing countries and donors will need a forum in which to debate the country’s security needs and priorities. Security coordination within the AU mission has often proven a challenge, but the mission’s guiding framework helped ensure that its contributors adhered to a basic common strategy. The government should now establish a new forum that would meet regularly to coordinate with its bilateral partners, enabling Mogadishu to impress upon them the country’s main security requirements and hopefully curbing the pursuit of individual interests by troop-contributing states. Somalia’s security partners in turn should focus on fulfilling their security roles and avoid meddling in local politics in their areas of operation. A forum could also be an opportunity for the government to detail a national plan for Somalia’s future security, which would help assuage local concerns that a transition might leave some parts of the country better protected than others. Without effective coordination, bilateral security relationships could hasten the country’s fragmentation by fracturing it into various zones of influence that overlap with Somalia’s current divisions between the federal authorities and assertive member states. Furthermore, there is a risk that powerful partners might look to Mogadishu to provide exclusive concessions – economic or otherwise – in return for military assistance. Better coordination with multiple partners will help the Somali authorities handle these demands and keep the focus on making the country safe. With negotiations on the AU mission’s next mandate set to kick off at the UN Security Council by December, Somalia would benefit greatly from having a plan and buy-in from security partners in place by then. What Should Happen Now? Somalia’s multilateral security system has been limping toward its finale for several years. Establishing a new model without the UN support office and possibly the AU mission will be arduous; a series of bilateral security relationships is unlikely to match what multilateral deployments have achieved. Current funding and geopolitical realities, however, make this shift the most realistic option beyond 2027. The government should be using the time it has to make this change work. A clear grasp of the challenges ahead would be a good place to start. Diplomats from some of Mogadishu’s security partners say both the government and the AU expect that further compromises can be hammered out over the future of UNSOS. If so, that confidence is misplaced. The Trump administration appears intent on seeing the end of the UN support mission, even if it has signalled that more time is available to allow for a smoother transition. It is also hard to gauge how much UNSOS will be able to do in 2027 as it focuses on its liquidation. Rather than assume business as usual, Mogadishu and its partners should use the temporary reprieve they have been granted to construct a new security system that can kick into action as early as the second half of 2027. The Somali government should urgently convene its security partners to establish a broad division of responsibilities and priorities to follow the departure of UNSOS. Setting out a viable plan for the country after UN support winds down also has a better chance of attracting fresh donor backing. A shift primarily to bilateral support is still a temporary measure, and it should only buy time for a lasting solution to the country’s troubles: a Somali government that can manage its own security needs. Mogadishu’s shortcoming in achieving this goal, despite two decades of foreign support, is rooted in entrenched political divisions rather than just financial and technical challenges. In the short term, the government should be ready to deploy troops to areas likely to be vacated by foreign troops; it should launch major new offensives only once the transition has been consolidated. But for the security transition to work over the long term, Somalia’s government and political class must address their political divisions and row in the same direction. They could start to do so by resolving the dispute regarding the timing and format for elections, continuing by concluding these polls swiftly so that an incoming administration with a clear mandate can take office. The new administration should make preparing for a security transition an overriding priority. It should lay out a plan for how Somali forces can take over from foreign troops, including by bringing federal member states into discussions regarding the future of Somali security. Such a plan is the best way to realise the country’s full sovereignty – an oft-stated ambition of the Somali government. But the longer political disputes drag on, the greater the risk that the transition to Somali forces falters and Al-Shabaab resurges. The U.S. decision to pull the plug on UNSOS appears to be a defining act in the decline of Somalia’s multilateral security system. In its aftermath, short-term gains by Al-Shabaab look inevitable. But a well-managed transition should help mitigate any losses and lay the groundwork for Somalia’s eventual stability. Shrink the UN mloukili Mon, 09/21/2026 - 15:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Global 21 September 2026 1 minutes Shrink the UN Originally published in Foreign Affairs The Next Secretary-General Must Get Back to Basics Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Richard Gowan Program Director, Global Issues and Institutions https://twitter.com/RichardGowan1 Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy The United Nations, international officials sometimes joke, is always in crisis. Since its inception in 1945, the organization has had to navigate deep geopolitical tensions, devastating humanitarian disasters, and periodic budget shortfalls. But as world leaders gather in New York for the annual General Assembly high-level week, the UN appears to be in particularly bad shape. China, Russia, and the United States, three of the five veto-wielding powers that dominate the Security Council, have prevented it from acting on wars in Iran and Ukraine and civil conflicts in Myanmar and Sudan. Poor countries complain that donor states have not met their UN pledges on development spending. And the Trump administration halted most U.S. funding to UN activities last year, forcing the organization to cut back on its peacekeeping and relief efforts. With challenges mounting, an upcoming leadership transition may decide whether the UN can stabilize itself and perhaps even regain some credibility—or slide further into decrepitude. Current Secretary-General António Guterres plans to step down at the end of the year, having struggled to reverse the organization’s political fortunes in his decadelong tenure. He has spent much of his last two years in office grappling with staff reductions and other cost-cutting measures to ensure the UN secretariat does not go bankrupt on his watch. His has been a thankless task, but diplomats and UN officials hope a new leader will be able to take a longer-term approach to refreshing the institution and keeping governments committed to multilateralism. The small crop of candidates to succeed Guterres include senior UN trade official Rebeca Grynspan, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi, and Guyana’s Ambassador to the UN Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett. Regardless of who wins, Guterres' successor will need to develop a new playbook for revitalizing the organization. Any serious effort must acknowledge an unpleasant reality: as long as the world remains competitive and chaotic, the UN’s ability to forge wide-ranging international agreements will remain constrained.
