On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/25/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out cthuratong Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:39 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Gender and Conflict 25 September 2026 1 minute What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out Originally published in TIME Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Cristal Downing Project Director, Gender and Conflict https://twitter.com/cristaldowning?lang=en Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Global Wars exact a heavy toll on women and yet, too often their voices and concerns are pushed to the margins of global peacemaking. Since the end of the Cold War, the United Nations has made halting but real progress in bringing women into peace negotiations and postwar reconstruction from Guatemala to Bangsamoro and beyond. Now that progress is being reversed. As peacemaking organizations fracture and lose their ability to press warring groups toward compromise, an assortment of social conservatives and warlords is finding new ways to exclude women from discussions about war and peace. Finding space for gender diversity could do more than ensure that women are heard; it could also give peace efforts a better chance of success. About a decade ago, Colombia’s peace process culminated in an agreement that seemed to offer a lesson in how to end a deeply rooted conflict. Negotiators brought in the belligerents but they also consulted civil society groups on rural reform, inclusive governance, and accountability for wartime atrocities, including sexual violence. Women’s groups had a voice in these discussions. The full article can be read on the TIME website. Arresting the Dangerous Descent Back into War in Northern Ethiopia eschelhaas Fri, 09/25/2026 - 14:01 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Members of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on September 23, 2026, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia after Tigrayan rebels seized control of airports in the region. AFP Statement / Africa 25 September 2026 9 minutes Arresting the Dangerous Descent Back into War in Northern Ethiopia Long-simmering tensions have turned to large-scale fighting after armed opposition groups in Tigray, Amhara and Afar launched a multi-pronged offensive against Ethiopian government forces. It is not too late to avert a return to costly, bloody war. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Northern Ethiopia is slipping into renewed war. After months of building tensions, on 23 September large-scale hostilities broke out between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and Amhara Fano militias, on one side, and the federal government and allied Tigrayan forces on the other. Responsibility for the escalation lies primarily with the TPLF, which launched ground assaults in coordination with other rebels with whom it has joined hands in a new alliance that vows to overthrow Ethiopia’s government. The upsurge in fighting comes almost five months after the TPLF retook power in the Tigray region, dealing a blow to a 2022 peace deal that had ended the last Tigray war and leading Addis Ababa to mount an intensifying drone campaign against TPLF forces. Much is unclear about how the two sides are faring on the battlefield, but many fear that further escalation in Tigray could draw in Eritrea, which is now closely aligned with the TPLF. Fighting in northern Ethiopia could also fuse dangerously with the war raging across the border in Sudan. African leaders backed by the U.S. and other outside powers should urge both sides to de-escalate and return to the negotiating table before hostilities spiral into a full-blown war that inflicts yet more suffering on civilians, while threatening to embroil other states. A Shaky Deal Gives Way The last war between the TPLF and Abiy’s federal government was one of the deadliest in the 21st century to date, killing hundreds of thousands. The roots of the conflict lie in the dramatic ascent of Abiy Ahmed to power in 2018. Abiy’s political base is in the Oromia region. His rise to the premiership ended the TPLF’s heavy-handed rule, and its decades-long political dominance, but also presaged a new struggle to come. TPLF leaders decamped to Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle to regroup. Full-scale war erupted in 2020, when TPLF forces launched a surprise attack on the federal military’s northern command post. Momentum swung both ways before Abiy and his coalition gained the upper hand in 2022. Under heavy military pressure, the TPLF agreed to a deal in November of that year ending the fighting. Under that accord, signed in Pretoria, the TPLF promised to disarm, and the parties agreed that Tigray would have an interim administration governing with the approval of both sides. While welcomed for bringing the conflict to an end, the Pretoria deal left a number of open wounds. While welcomed for bringing the conflict to an end, the Pretoria deal left a number of open wounds . The TPLF felt aggrieved by what it considered a lopsided settlement and, according to the government, it failed to honour its disarmament pledge. Eritrea, which had overcome enmity with the federal government to join the anti-TPLF campaign, felt it had been inadequately consulted on the final deal and wished the government had pushed to achieve a full battlefield victory. The status of hotly contested territories that the Amhara region had seized from Tigray during the conflict was left unresolved – leaving Tigrayans displaced from these areas languishing in temporary camps. Shoring up the wobbly settlement would have required patient statecraft from outside actors pressing the former belligerents to compromise, but the diplomacy that occurred was unavailing. Instead, the deal slowly collapsed. In late April and early May, the TPLF ousted Tigray’s interim administration and reinstalled its head Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president. After wresting back control of the region, TPLF leaders launched a major conscription drive and made a series of comments suggesting that their goal is to remove Abiy from power. They also repeatedly warned of an imminent return to war. Dialogue between the TPLF and other key rebel groups to form an alliance also accelerated, though these groups have little in common besides opposition to the government. The federal government, which was already cutting off federal funds and restricting fuel to the region as relations with the TPLF went into a rapid decline, began to launch occasional drone strikes on targets in Tigray. Shuttle diplomacy between Addis Ababa and Mekelle by the African Union’s envoy, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the 2022 peace talks, appeared to make little progress toward direct negotiations or an off-ramp. Regional tensions further poisoned the waters. Fuelled by its bitterness over the Pretoria agreement, and in line with the byzantine nature of alliance building in the region, Eritrea is now quietly aligned with its former enemy the TPLF. Meanwhile, Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of playing a central role in coordinating the opposition alliance that has formed against it. There is also a Sudan angle. Ethiopia’s leaders are furious at the Sudanese army for hosting thousands of Tigrayan fighters in territory under its control, whom they fear could attack Ethiopia from across the border or return to Tigray to join in battling the government. Many of these fighters have aided Khartoum in its own civil war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Seeing the Sudanese army as part of a regional axis coordinating with Ethiopian opposition forces, Addis Ababa has reportedly responded by allowing arms flows to the RSF and permitting it to operate from Ethiopian territory near Sudan’s Blue Nile state, where the paramilitary has made a series of gains. Ethiopia is also a close ally of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which is widely seen (despite its denials) as the RSF’s main backer. Meanwhile, the UAE’s Saudi rivals are aligned with the Sudanese army, as are Egypt and Eritrea, both arch-foes of Ethiopia. Diplomats and mediators say the superheated regional climate – in which both continental and Gulf powers are lining up on different sides of the Horn’s overlapping conflicts – has made it an uphill struggle to ward off a return to war in northern Ethiopia. Growing Tensions and a Return to War Tensions only increased over the course of August and September. As the culmination of its coalition-building efforts, on 20 September, the TPLF announced it was forming an Alliance for Survival with six other groups, most prominently a major umbrella organisation of the Amhara Fano rebel movement, which launched an insurgency against the government in August 2023. A statement launching the alliance set out its objective as overthrowing Abiy’s government . Then, on 22 September, the federal government responded with its biggest drone attack since August, targeting an apparent build-up of Tigrayan forces close to the Wollo area of the Amhara region where several anti-government groups are active. By 23 September, large-scale ground fighting between the TPLF and government forces had begun, with the former taking over three Tigray airports that had been still under federal control in Mekelle and the major towns of Axum and Shire, replacing the federal police stationed with their own forces without a fight. The federal government cancelled all flights to the Tigray region. The multi-front offensive appears to be the first attempt by the new opposition alliance to carry out coordinated military action against the federal government. Fighting in the north is now concentrated in two main areas. One is in the Amhara region close to the boundary with Southern Tigray, where Tigrayan forces and Amhara Fano launched a ground assault on federal forces on 23 September. The other hotspot is the boundary between Tigray and the Afar region to the east, where on the same day the TPLF launched an offensive against the government-backed anti-TPLF armed group the Tigray Peace Forces. Adding another combustible element, an anti-government group from Afar also joined the fray, fighting alongside the TPLF in two locations on the Tigray-Afar border. The multi-front offensive appears to be the first attempt by the new opposition alliance to carry out coordinated military action against the federal government. Government officials and several diplomats blamed the TPLF for the erupting conflict. Getachew Reda, the former senior Tigrayan official who is now an adviser to Abiy, accused the TPLF of starting a new war. The U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia, Ervin Massinga, also put out a statement expressing “disappointment” with the “large-scale offensive” launched by the TPLF. Other sources in Ethiopia appear to confirm that the TPLF launched the major new assaults, in coordination with other groups. In a statement , the TPLF claimed that its actions were “defensive” in nature, responding to the government’s “open invasion” on 22 September when it launched its barrage of drone strikes on Tigrayan military targets. Situation Report At the time of publication, the heaviest fighting is centred in the North Wollo area in the Amhara region, near the boundary with Tigray, where the TPLF and Fano elements appear to be coordinating their offensive against federal positions. With the Tigrayans and Fano reportedly taking territory and threatening several major towns in northern parts of Amhara, including Weldiya and Lalibela, all eyes are on the federal government’s response. The situation looks set to deteriorate as the government throws more troops and weaponry at beating back the TPLF and its allies, though few believe the opposition groups have the punch to pose a direct threat to the federal authorities in Addis Ababa. Should the government manage to halt or reverse the offensives beyond Tigray, a key question will then be whether Addis Ababa launches a large-scale ground war to remove the TPLF from power in Mekelle and restore federal control of most of Tigray. Privately, a senior government official stated that Addis Ababa will now seek to eliminate the TPLF as a threat, though another official suggested that the government would prefer to avoid a full-fledged war. To date, Abiy has appeared hesitant to get sucked into such a war in Tigray, but he may decide he has little alternative. Beyond the risk of setting off an unpredictable spiral, a major escalation could also push the fighting close to the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, creating the potential for interstate conflict. There is also a risk of conflict erupting along the Sudan-Ethiopia border, in effect merging the two countries’ conflicts, given the federal government’s and TPLF’s ties to rival belligerents there. A major incursion into Tigray by the federal government would also almost assuredly lead to extensive destruction, displacement and mass casualties – in short, a humanitarian disaster. Key African leaders ... as well as past and present heads of state ... should urgently push both sides to de-escalate and pursue an off-ramp into direct talks. Given the bad blood between the Ethiopian belligerents, outside engagement in the form of high-level diplomacy will likely be needed to prevent a plunge back into all-out conflict. Many have a role to play. Key African leaders, including Obasanjo (in his capacity as the AU’s High Representative for the Horn of Africa), as well as past and present heads of state, such as Kenyan President William Ruto and former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, should urgently push both sides to de-escalate and pursue an off-ramp into direct talks. These leaders should urge the TPLF to halt its offensives and take its grievances to the negotiating table, while they should also engage with Abiy to avoid a major new ground invasion of Tigray and to allow time for emergency diplomacy. By way of support, Saudi Arabia should push its allies in Asmara, Khartoum and Cairo, all of which have significant disputes with Addis Ababa, to avoid meddling and further inflaming the situation. For its part, the UAE should press its allies in Addis Ababa toward diplomacy and avoid fanning the flames with large new arms transfers. The U.S., which has shuttled between Addis and Mekelle and backed Obasanjo’s mediation, as well as key European powers, should back all these efforts through their own continued outreach, including to the traditionally highly insular Eritrean government. Averting a Nightmare Scenario With wars already raging nearby in Somalia, Sudan and Yemen, not to mention those beyond, a major new conflict in Ethiopia is a nightmare scenario. The humanitarian consequences are potentially horrific – all the more so given what northern Ethiopia has already experienced in recent years – and there is a non-trivial risk that other countries get dragged into what could become a regional conflagration . A window is still open for averting these outcomes – but absent urgent diplomacy, it could close all too soon. Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. Central African Republic: ICC Verdict in Seleka Commander Case. Click to expand Image Mahamat Said Abdel Kani during closing statements in the courtroom of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, November 25, 2025. © 2025 ICC-CPi (The Hague) – The International Criminal Court (ICC)’s conviction of Mahamat Said Abdel Kani for crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic offers an important measure of long-awaited justice for victims of the abusive Seleka armed group, Human Rights Watch said today. In 2012, the predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels ousted the Central African Republic president, François Bozizé, and seized power through a campaign of violence and terror. In March 2013, the Seleka took control of Bangui, the capital, attacking civilians and pillaging the city. In late 2013, Christian and animist militias known as anti-balaka, began to organize counterattacks against the Seleka. Both the Seleka and anti-balaka have been implicated in widespread atrocities against civilians. “As the first ICC verdict against a high-level Seleka commander, the judgment against Said is a significant milestone in the fight against impunity for serious crimes in the Central African Republic,” said Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “But this should only be considered a first step. The verdict is also a stark reminder of the ongoing abuses in the country, and the need for increased support for both international and domestic justice efforts to end the accountability gap that helps fuel recurring cycles of violence.” ICC judges convicted Said for crimes committed at the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry (Office Central de Répression du Banditisme, OCRB) in Bangui between April and August 2013. The crimes include imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, other inhumane acts, and persecution. Said was acquitted on the charges of war crimes. The majority of the judges found that the ouster of François Bozizé in March 2013 ended the conflict that had begun between the Seleka and the Central African armed forces in 2012, and therefore, there was no conflict at the time the alleged crimes were committed. Said was also acquitted for some incidents related to the crimes against humanity charges, including for lack of sufficient evidence. The court laid out a timeline for the sentencing proceedings, which will include a hearing in November. The court should take all necessary steps to ensure that affected communities in the Central African Republic learn about the judgment and next steps, including any appeals and reparations proceedings, Human Rights Watch said. Said is believed to have joined the Seleka in 2012 and was promoted to lieutenant, colonel, and then commander. In April 2013, when Seleka abuse in Bangui was acute, he was given a key role in the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry. The agency is a police unit created in the late 1990s to address a rise in banditry, which developed a reputation for abuse. Its abuse continues today and the government uses the unit at times to warn government critics of potential consequences of their criticism. Said was arrested in the Central African Republic and surrendered to the ICC on January 24, 2021. The court’s judges had issued an under-seal arrest warrant against him on January 7, 2019. In 2014, the Seleka splintered into several groups, including the Popular Front for the Renaissance (Front populaire pour la renaissance de la Centrafrique, FPRC), headed by Noureddine Adam and Michel Djotodia. Some factions of the FPRC aligned themselves with anti-balaka forces. Djotodia, who is sanctioned by the US Treasury, lives in Benin but returned to Bangui in 2020 for a short stay and is sometimes back in the country. Adam is reported to be between Chad and Sudan, where he continues to evade justice. On July 28, 2022, the ICC unsealed an arrest warrant against Adam, which was first issued against him under seal on January 7, 2019. ICC member countries should make every effort to support the court in arresting Adam and bring him to justice, Human Rights Watch said. Other high-profile Seleka leaders, such as Mahamat Al Khatim, Saleh Zabadi, and Ali Darassa, continue to lead splinter Seleka groups. In July 2025, ICC judges convicted two anti-balaka leaders, Alfred Yékatom and Patrice-Edouard Ngaïssona, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic between December 2013 and August 2014. Yékatom and Ngaïssona were sentenced to 15 and 12 years in prison, respectively, and appeals are ongoing. Another anti-balaka commander, Maxim Mokom, was surrendered to the court in March 2022, but the prosecution withdrew the charges against him in October 2023, citing a lack of evidence and witnesses. The ICC opened the investigation into crimes committed in the Central African Republic since 2012, following a request from the Central African Republic government in 2014. This was the ICC’s second investigation into crimes committed in the country. The first investigation related to an earlier conflict, in 2002 and 2003, and resulted in the acquittal of Jean-Pierre Bemba, a former vice president from the Democratic Republic of Congo. In December 2022, the ICC prosecutor announced the completion of his office’s investigative activities in the Central African Republic. ICC investigations in the Central African Republic have been complemented by proceedings before the Special Criminal Court in Bangui, staffed by international and Central African judges and prosecutors. The court has issued verdicts in four cases and has several ongoing proceedings and investigations. This critical justice avenue is facing significant financial challenges. International partners should provide the court with the resources it needs to fulfill its important mandate, Human Rights Watch said. Said’s verdict comes at a time when the ICC is facing extreme pressure. In February 2025, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order authorizing sanctions on ICC officials and others supporting the court’s work. Since then, the US government has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and staff, a UN expert, and three leading Palestinian human rights organizations. Together with three other human rights groups, Human Rights Watch has sued the Trump administration in a US court over its sanctions targeting the ICC. On July 13, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced an escalated campaign to “dismantle” the court, including an increased use of sanctions and pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. “The ICC is a critical court of last resort to deliver justice for the most serious crimes in the Central African Republic and across its docket,” Mudge said. “ICC member countries should redouble their efforts to protect the ICC and those supporting its work, so it can deliver on its essential global mandate.”

Russia Crackdown on Bypassing Online Censorship. Click to expand Image A person checks their phone in the Red Square in Moscow, Russia, March 31, 2026. © 2026 Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo (Berlin, September 24, 2026) – Russian authorities are doubling down on their efforts to quash freedom of expression, including access to information, by increasingly suppressing tools to circumvent draconian censorship laws, Human Rights Watch said today. Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) services face intensifying blocking and takedowns from app stores. “The Russian government’s escalating attacks on censorship circumvention services is part of its broader assault on access to information, privacy, and freedom of expression,” said Hugh Williamson, Europe and Central Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “These repressive tactics affect millions of people in Russia seeking to connect to the internet without state censorship.” On August 4, 2026, Exploit media outlet reported that 20 Virtual Private Network (VPN) providers in Russia had faced service disruptions caused by the blockings carried out by the Russian authorities. A representative of one of the affected VPN services told Human Rights Watch that the recent waves of blocking targeted VPN services’ infrastructure, namely, large blocks of IP addresses they use, including entire subnets of IP addresses allocated to them by their hosting service providers. Restoring VPN services following such bulk blocking can take more time and be more costly in comparison to previous more granular state blocking, the representative said. In June, the authorities carried out a coordinated attack targeting Amnezia VPN, one of the most popular VPN services in Russia. One of Amnezia’s developers said that the authorities blocked its IP addresses in bulk, targeted employees with phishing emails in an attempt to obtain sensitive data, and used distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, which overwhelmed the service and disrupted its work. It took Amnezia one and a half months to fully restore its services. The new tactics in state crackdown on VPNs have created significant technical, financial, and operational challenges and damaged their reputation as reliable services, Human Rights Watch said. In April, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media instructed more than 20 of the largest internet companies, which together provide digital services to the vast majority of Russians, to gather information on their clients’ VPN use and deny access to services when detecting VPN connections. According to a study published by RKS Global, a group of experts working on internet freedom, at least 30 of the largest Russian apps gathered this information. An expert at RKS Global told Human Rights Watch that the information included IP addresses used by the VPN services and was used in the recent attack on VPNs’ infrastructure. Over the past decade, VPNs have become a lifeline for accessing millions of censored websites in Russia, including to access independent media, foreign social media and messaging platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, and WhatsApp. Since spring 2025, the authorities have increasingly carried out “whitelists” shutdowns, blocking access to all but state approved websites. The 2017 law on VPN services prohibited them from providing access to state-blocked websites. By February 2026, the authorities had blocked at least 469 VPNs under this law. In 2025, the authorities banned advertising VPNs, introduced fines for “intentionally” searching for “extremist” content on the internet, including via VPNs, and classified the use of VPNs as an aggravating circumstance with regard to certain crimes. Nevertheless, the number of VPN downloads consistently grows, and about 40 percent of Russia’s population—57 million people—are estimated to use VPN. In addition to direct blocking, Russian authorities increasingly pressure foreign technology companies to take down VPN apps from their app stores, Human Rights Watch said. In its transparency report, Apple said that in 2025 it removed 468 “utility” applications, which includes VPNs, from its App Store. Overall, 1,213 applications were removed in response to Russian government requests, nearly 60 percent of all such removals globally. In March 2026, Apple removed several popular VPNs—Streisand, V2Box, v2RayTun, Happ, and Proxy Utility—from its App Store. v2RayTun shared Apple’s removal notification, which cited a demand from Roskomnadzor, the state media and communications watchdog, on the grounds that the application “included content that is illegal in Russia.” The notice referred to part 7 of article 15.1 of Russia’s Law on Information, which the Russian authorities widely use to restrict privacy, freedom of expression, and access to information online. In March 2026, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media ordered the four largest mobile service providers in the country to stop allowing payments to Apple account holders using mobile phone billing, a popular method for paying for VPNs. In July, Human Rights Watch sent a letter to Apple, inquiring about company policy on VPN takedowns in Russia, as well as the exact number of VPNs taken down by Apple on the authorities’ demand. Apple responded that “[Apple is] required to follow the law everywhere we operate, even where we may disagree with a country’s laws. In Russia, failure to comply with lawful orders could result in Apple no longer being able to operate the App Store or distribute content in the country, and we believe that would not be in the best interests of our users, because the App Store remains an important platform for Russian users to access information.” Russian authorities also repeatedly demanded that Google take down hundreds of VPN apps from its Play Store. In February, a Russian court fined Google 22.8 million rubles (around USD 300,000) for failure to remove VPN apps as authorities ordered. In July, both Apple and Google faced apparent blocking in Russia. VPNs that do not collect their clients’ logs, or digital footprint, and do not transfer data to state authorities can ensure privacy of internet communications for their users, including against the advanced state surveillance system in Russia, Human Rights Watch said. By escalating their blocking of VPNs, the authorities push users to repeatedly change VPN service providers, with privacy and security risks, such as choosing a VPN service that stores data without their consent, or shares data with Russian authorities. Multiple United Nations human rights institutions condemn restrictions on anonymity, including the blocking of VPNs, that are essential for safeguarding rights online, as violating the right to privacy, freedom of expression, access to information, the right to peaceful assembly, and other rights and freedoms. The 2015 UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression said in a report that anonymity and encryption are key for freedom of opinion and expression, and that blanket prohibitions fail necessity and proportionality criteria. Foreign technology companies should resist Russian government pressure to take down VPNs from their app stores. Governments, intergovernmental institutions, groups, and foundations concerned with promoting human rights including freedom of expression, access to information, and other internet freedoms should continue developing and supporting the tools that maximize privacy, ensure anonymity, and enable internet users in Russia to circumvent draconian internet censorship. “With the government escalating attacks on digital rights, it is crucial for groups working to ensure uncensored access to the internet in Russia receive financial, institutional, and other essential support,” Williamson said.

Niger Rejects Key Rights Recommendations at UN Review. Niger has rejected key recommendations raised by United Nations member countries during its Universal Periodic Review (UPR) earlier this year, including calls to address arbitrary detention, discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people, and accountability for serious human rights violations. The UPR is a UN Human Rights Council process in which the human rights records of member states are reviewed by other member countries every five years. Click to expand Image Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani of Niger attends the Alliance of Sahel States second summit on security and development, in Bamako, Mali, December 23, 2025. © 2025 Mali Government Information Center via AP On September 1, Niger’s military junta responded to the 265 recommendations made in May by 97 UN member countries and accepted 254 of them, including commitments to strengthen civilian protection and ensure security forces receive training on international human rights and humanitarian law. The junta however rejected 11 recommendations addressing some of the country’s most pressing rights concerns, including to reverse its June decision to start the withdrawal process from the International Criminal Court (ICC). Leaving the ICC risks depriving victims of grave international crimes a last resort to seek justice and remedies. The junta also rejected calls to release people held arbitrarily, including ousted President Mohamed Bazoum and his wife. The government said their cases fall exclusively under national jurisdiction and denied that anyone is arbitrarily detained. In February 2025, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Bazoum and his wife’s detention was arbitrary and called for their immediate release. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Court of Justice had reached a similar conclusion in December 2023. Niger also rejected recommendations to repeal the law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offense and to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, citing “cultural, social, and religious sensitivities.” The rejection is particularly concerning following the junta’s adoption of a new penal code in March criminalizing consensual same-sex relations with up to 10 years’ imprisonment, contrary to its regional and international human rights obligations. These rejections come amid a broader crackdown since the military seized power in 2023. Authorities have severely restricted political activity, curtailed media freedom, and targeted civil society activists, journalists and political opponents. The prominent rights defender Moussa Tiangari has been arbitrarily detained since December 2024. Niger needs to meaningfully engage with UPR recommendations by fully implementing those it accepted and addressing the serious rights concerns raised in those it rejected.

Ethiopia: Indiscriminate Airstrike in Tigray. Click to expand Image A collapsed wall in a residential house following the August 20, 2026 airstrike on a residential compound in Daero neighborhood, Mekelle, Tigray region, Ethiopia. The image was taken the same day by a Mekelle resident. © 2026 Private (Nairobi) – An apparent Ethiopian government airstrike on a residential compound in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region on August 20, 2026, should be investigated as a possible war crime, Human Rights Watch said today. The attack wounded 13 civilians, including seven children. The airstrike hit the Daero neighborhood of Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, which had no evident military targets, making the strike unlawfully indiscriminate. Ethiopian authorities should impartially and transparently investigate the attack, prosecute those responsible for any wrongdoing, and adequately compensate the victims. “The resumption of hostilities in northern Ethiopia heightens concerns about unlawful attacks and the grave threat posed to civilians,” said Laetitia Bader, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “To prevent further harm to civilians, the Ethiopian military needs to abide by the laws of war and ensure that they take all feasible precautions before carrying out any attack.” Between August 21 and September 6, Human Rights Watch interviewed three survivors of the Daero attack, two medical workers, and two residents who visited the site. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery and verified photographs and videos depicting the attack site and remnants of an air-dropped munition. Additional photographs and descriptions of blast and fragmentation injuries were consistent with the detonation of an air-dropped general-purpose bomb. Human Rights Watch contacted and wrote to the army’s spokesperson with key questions but at publication had received no response. On the same day as the attack on the compound, a second airstrike hit Quiha, a neighborhood near Mekelle’s airport that has been used for military purposes. There were no reported casualties in the second strike. The strikes occurred amid renewed clashes between the Ethiopian federal government and forces of Tigray’s main political party, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which fought during the 2020-2022 armed conflict. The parties had signed an African Union-mediated cessation of hostilities agreement in November 2022. Heavy fighting erupted between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan forces on August 1 near the country’s border with Sudan, and sporadic clashes have continued. Tigrayan regional authorities have accused the federal government of carrying out several airstrikes causing civilian casualties. On September 21, a drone struck an aid convoy in Tigray, which the United States government condemned. On September 23, Tigrayan forces controlled key regional airports, leading Ethiopian airlines to suspend flights. Fighting intensified in Tigray, and spread to the Amhara and Afar regions, pitting federal forces against several armed groups, including Tigrayan forces. Daero residents said that on August 20, shortly after 11 a.m., they saw a likely fighter jet drop a munition that struck an open area in a residential compound for teachers and their families. Residents provided accounts and photos of collapsed walls, doors, and ceilings as the detonation’s blast wave significantly damaged concrete block houses surrounding the impact area. Click to expand Image A damaged residential house after the August 20, 2026 airstrike on a residential compound in Daero neighborhood, Mekelle, Tigray region, Ethiopia. The image was taken the same day by a Mekelle resident. © 2026 Private One survivor, who suffered a blast-related soft tissue injury and a deep scalp wound requiring surgery, said: “I was inside with my family when I heard a very loud sound. I went out. A plane came lower and then climbed before it released a weapon. The explosion caused the wall of my compound to completely collapse.” Another survivor, whose four relatives were injured, said: “My children were in the kitchen. The explosion caused the house to fall on them. I had to dig three of them out from under the corrugated metal and wood.” A Mekelle resident who went to the site soon after the attack described seeing a “blackened crater” in the compound. The strike “had impacted around 10 houses on both sides of the [residential] block,” the resident said, and caused “holes in the walls [of the houses] struck by some kind of shrapnel.” A satellite image captured on September 1 shows a crater measuring about four meters in diameter and the collapsed wall of one house. Human Rights Watch also examined photographs and videos recorded by a witness on the day of the attack showing the strike’s aftermath. One video shows a crater in the courtyard and the same collapsed concrete wall visible in satellite imagery. Several photographs show gates and windows shattered by the blast, weapon remnants of various-sized steel fragments, and remnants of the bomb body within the crater. International humanitarian law, also called the laws of war, requires warring parties to distinguish between military objectives and civilians. Parties must take all feasible precautions to verify that targets are military objectives. Indiscriminate attacks, which strike military targets and civilians or civilian objects without distinction, including attacks not directed at a specific military objective, are prohibited. Individuals who commit serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent—that is, deliberately or recklessly—can be prosecuted for war crimes. Click to expand Image A large crater caused by an air-dropped munition in the courtyard of a residential compound in Daero neighborhood, Mekelle, Tigray region, Ethiopia, August 20, 2026. © 2026 Private Residents and witnesses said that they saw no Tigrayan fighters or other military presence at the compound or in the vicinity before or following the strike. Human Rights Watch found no evidence to support some public reporting suggesting that the Daero attack was a failed attempt to strike Tigrayan military and civilian leaders nearby. Residents said they rushed the wounded to Ayder Referral Hospital, Tigray’s largest public hospital, for treatment. Medical workers said they treated 13 patients with trauma wounds, including 10 with soft tissue or mild chest injuries, and 3 with more severe injuries, including a 12-year-old girl who had a complicated leg fracture that required surgery. Availability of medical care in Tigray is minimal. One medical worker said Ayder lacked basic supplies: “We have nothing … We’ve not received anything from the federal government for the last 4-5 months … lifesaving equipment, tubes, anesthesia and the like, unless patients buy from a private pharmacy, we can’t treat.” Two teachers said they were still living in damaged homes in the compound. Some families of those injured were struggling to afford medical treatment. One survivor whose daughter was harmed in the attack said: “The kids aren’t playing outside anymore. My injured daughter is still in the hospital. We buy everything from outside – the hospital only provides a bed. She needs medication daily, which we can’t afford.” Following the November 2022 truce, the African Union established a monitoring mechanism, but it has not reported publicly on abuses against civilians. The AU should urgently convene the parties under the agreement’s framework and ensure that the mechanism provides a robust human rights monitoring component and public reporting. The AU, the UN, concerned governments, and the AU mediator, former Nigerian President Olusegan Obasanjo, and other key leaders, should also publicly call on all warring parties, including those that haven’t signed the agreement, to protect civilians and facilitate impartial investigations into alleged war crimes, Human Rights Watch said. The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights should closely monitor the situation in Ethiopia, release regular public reports, and brief the UN Human Rights Council. Ethiopia should endorse the Political Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas. “The Ethiopian government is legally obligated to impartially investigate the airstrike in Daero and take appropriate action to reduce civilian harm,” Bader said. “Concerned governments should press all the warring parties to meet their international humanitarian law obligations and hold those responsible for abuses to account.”

Array of Experts Back Lawsuit Challenging Trump’s ICC Sanctions Regime. Click to expand Image Thurgood Marshall United States Federal Courthouse building in lower Manhattan, New York City. © 2026 Laura Prieto Uribe/Human Rights Watch (New York) – An array of former government officials, human rights groups, bar associations, and legal experts from around the world have filed eight amicus briefs supporting a lawsuit challenging US President Donald Trump’s executive order authorizing sanctions on International Criminal Court (ICC) officials, staff, and others affiliated with or assisting the court’s work. The American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute brought the suit on August 11, 2026. They subsequently sought a preliminary injunction to stop the sanctions, which they say illegally undermine access to justice for victims of serious international crimes and prevent civil society from working together to end impunity. The groups say in their suit that the sanctions are a blatantly illegal attack on international justice. The groups assert the sanctions have forced them to curtail a wide range of work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Their lawsuit also argues the sanctions exceed the president’s powers and are based on a false claim of a “national emergency,” arising out of the work of the ICC, that has no basis in fact. While the ICC has long been a target of opponents of international justice due to its investigations into atrocities, including in Libya, the Philippines, Sudan, and Ukraine, its Palestine investigation—which led to arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Minister of Defense Yoav Gallant and a Hamas official on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity—has sparked an escalated assault by the Trump administration on the institution and the rule of law. In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged to “dismantle” the court by, among other steps, increasing the use of sanctions. The administration has used the executive order to sanction ICC prosecutors, nine ICC judges including the court’s president, the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and three leading Palestinian human rights groups. The following groups have filed the amicus briefs: A coalition of 38 human rights organizations, including Amnesty International and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), details how the ICC sanctions have impaired civil society from supporting international justice efforts. Former US sanctions officials, including in the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), articulate why the Trump administration’s use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act (IEEPA) is a dangerous departure and how it undermines the credibility and effectiveness of US sanctions. The Brennan Center for Justice explains why the executive order and the resulting sanctions exceed the president’s authority under the National Emergency Act and IEEPA. Physicians for Human Rights outlines how the ICC sanctions have made it more difficult for victims of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes to pursue and secure justice. Former US ambassadors-at-large for global criminal justice and prosecutors of international criminal tribunals discuss the importance of the ICC to international justice, the necessity of judicial and prosecutorial independence within the ICC, and the important role that civil society plays within the justice system.The International Criminal Court Bar Association (ICCBA) argues that the sanctions threaten to undermine the independence of ICC lawyers and therefore pose a grave threat to the rule of law. The New York City Bar Association (NYCBA) asserts that the ICC is an essential component of international justice and that the executive order undermines judicial independence, interferes with the work of the legal profession, and impairs the administration of justice.Legal academics, professors, and practitioners whose teaching, scholarship, and professional engagement focus on international law and related fields describe how the sanctions impair their ability to teach, conduct research, and collaborate within the international legal sphere; chill academic freedom; and violate their First Amendment rights. Plaintiffs are represented by Foley Hoag LLP.

US: Trump Administration Rejects External Election Observers. Click to expand Image A voter filling out a ballot at the Green Spring Gardens polling station in Lincolnia, Virginia, US, June 20, 2023. © 2023 Minh Connors/The Washington Post via AP Photo (New York) – The Trump administration’s decision not to invite the leading international election observation body to monitor crucial US midterm polls fuels fears of serious human rights concerns around the upcoming elections, Human Rights Watch said today. “The US government has long criticized Russia and other governments for dodging external scrutiny of their elections,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director of Human Rights Watch. “Now the Trump administration is mimicking that behavior.” The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which has observed every US federal election since 2002, called the decision “regrettable” and “not in line with” US commitments. Just over a month before the elections, the United States is mired in several controversies that raise concerns about the rights of voters, Human Rights Watch said. The Supreme Court on September 25, 2026, granted an emergency appeal by the Trump administration to overturn a ruling that had temporarily barred the government from using the current version of the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database to verify voters’ citizenship. Since 2002, the OSCE has observed 12 rounds of elections in the United States, including six midterm elections. OSCE observers were invited to observe the 2018 midterms during President Donald Trump’s first term and issued a 38-page report at the time. Most recently, the organization observed the 2024 election, which brought President Trump into office for a second term. The organization deemed that election “well-run” and said that candidates campaigned “freely across the country,” with “voters engaging actively.” Human Rights Watch wrote to the State Department seeking comment on the OSCE’s September 23, 2026 press release but has not yet received a response. The Trump administration has previously threatened to quit the OSCE, and its ambassador to the OSCE, Darrell Owens, has been pushing an effort to “reform, refocus, and refine” the OSCE since his confirmation by the US Senate in June. This is the first time the United States has declined to invite in OSCE monitors since they began observing US elections. The OSCE Parliamentary Assembly president, Pere Joan Pons, said that the Trump administration’s decision “represents a significant departure from an established democratic practice.” It is notable that an administration ostensibly committed to combatting fraud is unwilling to invite external observers who have cultivated expertise in exactly this issue, Human Rights Watch said. The decision is a serious one, and its consequences will reverberate beyond the United States. The 57 OSCE participating countries all made a reciprocal commitment to support democratic elections by enabling trained monitors from other OSCE countries to monitor major elections in their countries. Most countries continue to abide by this commitment and work to implement the OSCE’s recommendations. The United States should be signaling to other governments how vital it is to uphold the rights of voters, not breaking with a tradition of cooperation, Human Rights Watch said. In recent years, the OSCE has been unable to monitor elections in Belarus, Georgia, and Tajikistan due to the refusal of these governments to engage with monitoring procedures in a timely way, and in Russia’s case a refusal to issue an invitation at all. In 2024, the United States issued a pointed critique of Russia for its noncooperation with the OSCE, saying that “for decades, the United States has invited OSCE observers to assess our own elections and encouraged fellow participating States to do the same. We value the thorough, professional, impartial assessments of the OSCE observers and we take their recommendations seriously.” The lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections in the US has been accompanied by a series of new federal policies which, if implemented, could make access to polling places more difficult and limit US voters’ ability to exercise their right to vote. Trump and senior officials in his administration have been advancing a largely debunked claim that the outcomes of US elections have been affected by widespread noncitizen voting. The administration’s rhetoric has often implied, without any evidentiary basis, that state and local officials have deliberately conspired to push noncitizens to vote unlawfully. The US Department of Justice has sent letters to local election officials warning them of the risk of criminal prosecution if they allow noncitizen voting and have been pressuring states to use the SAVE database to screen their voter rolls. Continued use of the database, which the Supreme Court greenlighted on September 25, could lead states to wrongfully block people from voting. Reliance on this incomplete source has already incorrectly flagged some naturalized citizens’ voter registrations for further scrutiny. Practically, these flags create barriers to access the polls since only some people are being asked to meet administrative burdens and provide additional proof of citizenship. The Trump administration is also proceeding with plans to send about 1,000 monitors to midterm polling places. This move has sparked concern because the effort is framed around preventing ineligible people from voting, rather than ensuring that eligible voters are able to cast their ballots. Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon, a Republican, expressed concern about the “aggressive” conduct of some Justice Department monitors during the primary cycle. That track record raises concerns about whether their presence during the general election will deter some people from voting, Human Rights Watch said.
